review.impact: `checkPlanRun` drops the result of `parseSpec`'s `problems`. If `spec.md` is missing, it passes `''`. A run with no spec, or with a spec that has no sections, can pass `werk check` with exit 0 when no ticket lists a story. Only `runPlan` enforces spec validity, so the `plan` and `check` commands give different verdicts for the same run.
review.fix: Parse the spec once in `checkRun`, or pass the parsed `Spec` to it. Add a failed result such as `spec-usable`, with the spec problems as its detail, to the verdict. Then `ok` and `describeFailures` report a missing or unusable spec in both commands.

review.impact: The CLI builds the single-ticket verdict itself. It filters `verdict.own`, makes a fake verdict with `set: []`, and picks `one.ok` over `verdict.ok`. The plan module owns the verdict rules, but this rule lives in the CLI. Other callers, such as a future server endpoint, must copy it, and the copies can drift.
review.fix: Add a function to `plan/run.ts` or `plan/checks.ts` that returns `{ ok, lines }` or an error string for a run and an optional ticket number. Then the `check` case only prints the lines and exits, the same as the `plan` case uses `Outcome`.

review.impact: `JSON.parse` of `plan.json` has no guard. If the file is damaged, or has no `root`, `werk check` stops with an uncaught stack trace. It does not give the `werk: ...` error that the other failures give. `proposeAnswers` guards the same kind of parse.
review.fix: Wrap the parse in try/catch. Check that `root` is a string. If either check fails, return `plan.json of run <run> is not usable` as the error string.

review.impact: `checkRun` parses every ticket in `titled`. Then `ownChecks` parses each ticket again from its text, and line 29 parses it a third time to get the title. The ticket shape is parsed in three places, so a future change to `parseTicket` options must be made at each call.
review.fix: Parse each file once. Pass the parsed `Ticket` and its raw text to `ownChecks`, then take the title from that parsed ticket.

review.impact: `checkRun` parses each ticket text three times: once for `titled`, once more for `title` in `own`, and a third time inside `ownChecks`. The three parses can drift apart if one call site changes, and the reader must check that they agree.
review.fix: Parse each file once into a `Ticket`. Pass that `Ticket` to `ownChecks` instead of `(number, text)`, and take `title` from it. `filePaths` still needs the raw text, so pass the text next to the ticket.

review.impact: The single-ticket branch builds a fake verdict, `{ ...verdict, own: [one], set: [] }`, so that `describeFailures` prints only one ticket. It also has two parallel ternaries on `one`. Any new field on `Verdict` or new logic in `describeFailures` can break this branch without warning.
review.fix: Add a `describeOwnFailures(o: OwnVerdict)` helper in checks.ts. Have `describeFailures` call it, and have the CLI call it for one ticket. Then the CLI has one branch per case and builds no synthetic `Verdict`.

review.impact: No code reads `OwnVerdict.chars`. Only checks.json gets it. No code outside the tests reads `Ticket.checks` (ticket.ts:31) or `SetResult.cards` / `SetResult.stories` (sets.ts:24-25). These dead fields make readers think something uses them.
review.fix: Remove the fields that no code reads. If checks.json must hold `chars` for an outside consumer, add a comment that names that consumer.

review.impact: The code that writes `EventBody[]` to `.werk/log.jsonl` with `seq` and `at` appears in run.test.ts:67, in cli.test.ts:449, and with a different shape in scope.test.ts:6. The three copies can drift when the event envelope changes.
review.fix: Move a `writeLog(dir, bodies)` helper into test/harness.ts, or add a method on `TempProject`. Use it in run.test.ts and cli.test.ts.

review.impact: `numbers` is a `Set` with the same keys as `byNumber`, which the next line builds. One fact is stored two ways.
review.fix: Remove `numbers` and use `byNumber.has(b)`.

review.impact: No test covers the failure paths of `proposeAnswers`. These paths are a missing answers file, a file that is not JSON, JSON that is not an array, and an answer with a bad slug or an empty title. The most likely real failure is a writer that forgets `spec-answers.json` or `ticket-answers.json`. If any of these paths broke, for example by returning ok: true or by throwing on a missing file, every test still passes. The only tested failure is an id that already exists.
review.fix: Add a test to `run.test.ts` with a spec writer that writes `spec.md` but no answers file. Assert that `ok` is false and that the text contains 'the spec writer wrote no .werk/tickets/1000/spec-answers.json'. Add a second test with an answers file that holds `[{"slug":"Bad Slug","title":"x"}]` and assert the 'no kebab-case slug' line. Also cover a file that is not JSON and a JSON object that is not an array.

review.impact: The test name says that the check 'reads the map as it is now, and rewrites checks.json'. The test changes only a ticket file. It never changes the map, and it never reads checks.json after the second check. If `checkPlanRun` used a scope cached in plan.json, or stopped writing checks.json, this test still passes.
review.fix: Between the plan and the check, append a map event that changes the required set. For example, add and decide a new card under #plan. Then assert that the verdict fails `cards-cited` for that card. After `checkPlanRun`, parse checks.json again and assert that it holds the new verdict, for example `checks.own.length === 2`.

review.impact: No test covers a ticket writer that exits non-zero. No test covers a spec writer that exits 0 but writes no spec.md. Both are early returns with their own messages. A regression there, for example continuing to the checks after a failed ticket writer, goes unnoticed.
review.fix: In the 'a spec writer that fails' test, or in a new test, script the ticket writer as `[{ stderr: 'boom' }, { exit: 1 }]`. Assert that the text contains 'the ticket writer failed: claude exited 1: boom' and that the board is empty. Add a spec script that writes only `spec-answers.json`, and assert the 'wrote no .werk/tickets/1000/spec.md' line.

review.impact: No test calls `appendBoard` on a board log that already has events. So no test checks that `seq` continues from the last line, or that the earlier lines stay. Each run.test case starts with an empty board. A bug that restarts `seq` at 1 on every plan run, or that overwrites the file, is not caught.
review.fix: Add a test that calls `appendBoard` two times on the same project directory. Assert that the seq values are 1, 2, 3 across the calls, and that the first line of the file is unchanged byte for byte. The decision log test in cli.test.ts does the same check.

review.impact: The plan runs both headless writers with `--permission-mode acceptEdits` in the project directory. Card text goes into each prompt word for word. With that mode, a writer can edit any file in the project without approval. This includes `.werk/log.jsonl`, where it could write accepted cards directly and skip the ghost and ✓ step. It also includes `.werk/board.jsonl` and the source code. The prompt asks the writer to write only into the run directory, but the program does not check this. A wrong or prompt-injected writer can change the map without anyone seeing it.
review.fix: Limit what the writer can change. One way is to run each writer in a copy or temporary directory and copy back only the expected files from the run directory. Another way is to read the log, the board and the git working-tree state before and after each writer, then fail the plan if anything outside `.werk/tickets/<run>/` changed. As a minimum, pass a narrow `--allowedTools` list.

review.impact: `check <run>` accepts any text as the run, including `..` and absolute segments. `runDir` joins it under `.werk/tickets`, so `werk check ../../x` reads `plan.json` from outside the run directories and writes `checks.json` there. The user runs this command locally, so the risk is small, but the command can write outside `.werk/tickets/`.
review.fix: In `parseArgs`, accept only a run that matches `^\d+$`, which is the form `runPlan` writes (`now.getTime()`). Or check that `runDir(projectDir, run)` stays inside `.werk/tickets` before reading or writing.

review.impact: `proposeAnswers` checks only that `slug` and `title` are strings. A writer can return `why` or `body` as an object, a number or an array. The spread `...(answer.why ? { why: answer.why } : {})` then writes that value to the decision log, and `appendEvent` does not check field types. A non-string `why` or `body` can break the fold or the page, which expect strings.
review.fix: Require `why` and `body` to be strings when they are present (`typeof answer.why === 'string'`). Report any other answer as a bad answer, the same way as a bad slug.

review.impact: The subtree walk scans every link for each subtree card, and it calls `inside.includes` on each match. The cost is O(S × L × S) for S subtree cards and L links. The loop after it also calls `inside.includes` twice for each link. A map with a few thousand links and a large subtree makes `werk plan` and `werk check` do millions of extra operations. The cost grows with map size, not with the size of the plan.
review.fix: Build a `Map<parentId, childIds[]>` from the `refines` links one time. Keep a `Set` of the subtree ids next to the `inside` array. Then the walk does one lookup for each card, and each membership test is O(1).

review.impact: Nothing catches errors at the top level. A broken verb module makes `collectVerbs` throw, and a verb's `run` can throw or reject. In both cases the error leaves `main` as an unhandled top-level await rejection. The agent then gets a raw Bun stack trace, not a `werk:` message on stderr. One bad verb file also breaks every command, `werk help` included. Error output stops following the `werk: ...` form that `unknownVerbMessage` sets up.
review.fix: Wrap `main` in a try/catch at the top level. In the catch, write `werk: <error.message>` to stderr and set `process.exitCode = 1`. Each verb then needs no error handling of its own, and the output stays in one form.

review.impact: `process.exit()` runs right after `process.stderr.write`/`process.stdout.write`. If the stream is an async pipe, the output can be cut short. The file also differs from `src/cli.ts`, which sets `process.exitCode` and lets the process end on its own.
review.fix: Use `process.exitCode = verdict.ok ? 0 : 1` here. For the missing-file case, use `process.exitCode = 2` and return early, for example by moving the body into a function. Do not call `process.exit`.

review.impact: `loadVerbModules` imports every verb module at the start of every command, so each command loads the dependencies of all verbs. As verbs grow, for example a `werk serve` verb that pulls in Vite and React, simple verbs get slower, and an import error in one verb breaks all of them.
review.fix: Keep the one-file-per-verb registration, but make the import lazy. One option: derive the verb name from the file name and import only the matching module. Another option: verbs export light metadata, and `run` imports its heavy dependencies dynamically. Make this change before the first heavy verb arrives.

review.impact: One tsconfig type-checks both the Bun command line in `src/` and the browser client in `web/`. The `src/` code sees the `DOM` types, and `web/` sees the `bun` types. So a typecheck does not catch `document` used in command-line code, or `Bun.*` used in client code.
review.fix: Split the config into `tsconfig.json` with project references. Give `src/`+`e2e/` the `types: ["bun"]` setting and no DOM, and give `web/` the `DOM` lib and no bun types. Point `make typecheck` at `tsc -b`.

review.impact: The `record` lcov helper is written twice, here and in src/coverage/gate.test.ts:7, with different bodies. A change to the lcov format in the tests must be made in two places, and the two copies can drift apart.
review.fix: Move one `record` helper into a shared test module, for example src/coverage/lcov-fixture.ts, and import it in both test files.

review.impact: The `list` case copies the body of the `help` verb in src/verbs/help.ts. If the help output changes in one place, `werk` and `werk help` can print different text. Only the test in src/cli.test.ts would catch this.
review.fix: In the `list` case, run the `help` verb from the registry, or remove the `list` kind and make `resolve` return the `help` verb when there are no arguments.

review.impact: `formatVerbList` builds `left` as an array parallel to `verbs`, then reads it by index with `?? ''`. The fallback exists only to satisfy `noUncheckedIndexedAccess` and can never run, so it adds a branch that is never taken.
review.fix: Build pairs in one pass, for example `const rows = verbs.map((v) => [v.usage ?? v.name, v.summary] as const)`, then compute the width and the lines from `rows`.

review.impact: `$(subst test-coverage,test:coverage,$@)` hides a name mapping inside a text substitution. A new target whose script name differs from the target name needs another nested `subst`, and the rule becomes hard to read.
review.fix: Rename the package.json script to `test-coverage` so that each target name equals its script name, and use `bun run $@`. Or give `test-coverage` its own explicit rule.

review.impact: No test covers how `cli.ts` passes on an exit code from a verb. The only real verb is `help`, and it returns 0. A change that drops `return` in the `case 'verb'` branch, or that ignores a non-zero or async result, still passes every test. The `werk help` test still exits 0 when `process.exitCode` becomes `undefined`.
review.fix: Add a `cli.test.ts` case that needs a non-zero verb exit code. One option: make `VERBS_DIR` overridable through an environment variable, then run a fixture verb that returns 3 from an async `run`. Another option: move `main` into a pure function that takes the loaded verbs, then test it in process.

review.impact: Every test passes both an lcov path and a list of files. No test runs the defaults (`coverage/lcov.info` and `PURE_FILES`), and `make test-coverage` uses the defaults. A bug in the default path or in the `listed.length > 0 ? listed : PURE_FILES` fallback is not detected by any test.

review.impact: The `test.each` cases for a non-verb default export cover a missing `run`, a non-object and `null`. No case has a missing or non-string `name` or `summary`. review.impact: The preload tells the fake from the real agent by checking for the text 'fake claude' in the first 512 bytes of the file. That text lives in a shell comment in src/test/fake-claude/bin/claude and in the header that installFakeClaude writes. If someone rewords or removes that comment, the guard fails in one of two ways: it rejects the fake and stops every test run, or it accepts any file that happens to contain the phrase. Nothing in the code links the comment to the check.
review.fix: Put the marker in one exported constant, for example FAKE_MARKER in state.ts. Write it into both launcher scripts from that constant, or check the resolved path (realpath(found) === realpath(join(FAKE_BIN, 'claude'))) instead of the file content.

review.impact: The type Role lists every child role, but only Match.role uses it. roleFor, TurnContext.role and CallRecord.role are plain strings. A typo in WERK_AGENT_ROLE in werk code is recorded and matched without any error, so a script with `when: { role: 'builder' }` fails with 'no reply matches' and points to the wrong cause.
review.fix: Make roleFor return Role, and have it reject or flag an unknown env value. Type TurnContext.role and CallRecord.role as Role. Or remove the Role union and type Match.role as string, so the types do not suggest a check that does not exist.

review.impact: run() takes options only from the last argument. If an options object is in any other position, the filter drops it without an error. The test then runs with the wrong cwd, env or stdin, and the cause is hard to find.
review.fix: Throw when a non-string argument is not the last one. Or change the signature to run(cmd, args: string[], opts?: RunOptions).

review.impact: claimRecord counts the pass from the earlier records with the same role. readRecord returns undefined for a record that another process is writing at that moment. Two calls that start at the same time can then both get the same pass number, so the `when.pass` match picks the wrong reply for a parallel run.
review.fix: Write the record to a temporary file and rename it into place, so a reader never sees a partial file. Or retry readRecord when the parse fails, instead of skipping the record in the pass count.

review.impact: `const reply = script && chooseReply(script, ctx)` repeats a check that the top level already made: when script is undefined, finish(127) runs and the process exits. The extra `script &&` hides the narrowing and makes the reader think that playTurn can run with no script.
review.fix: Store the script in a const after the check, for example `const script: Script = readScript(state) ?? finish(127)`, so the type is Script inside playTurn. Then call chooseReply(script, ctx) directly.

review.impact: `checkStep` keeps its own list of step kinds: 'text', 'tool', 'write', 'ask', 'sleep', 'die' and 'event'. This list repeats the keys of the `Step` union and the `if`/`else` chain in `planTurn`. Suppose a new step kind is added to `Step` and to `planTurn` but not to this list. Then every step of that kind throws 'a step needs one kind'.
review.fix: Declare the kinds one time, for example `const STEP_KINDS = [...] as const`, next to `Step`. Use that constant in `checkStep`. Or add a test that compares the list with every branch in `planTurn`.

review.impact: The `ask` branch repeats the tool_use emission that the `call` helper at line 242 already does: it takes the next 'toolu' id and emits an `assistant` tool_use block. Each copy can change the event shape on its own. Then a permission ask and a plain tool call would produce different tool_use events.
review.fix: Split `call` into two helpers. One helper emits the tool_use event and returns its id. The other helper emits the tool result. The `ask` branch then calls only the first helper.

review.impact: `answerTo` casts the control_response message to its own type. `answerResult` in script.ts:225 casts the same message again to a different type. Two separate casts of one wire shape can disagree with no type error, because both start from `unknown`.
review.fix: In script.ts, export one `ControlResponse` type and one pure `parseControlResponse(line)` function. `answerTo` and `answerResult` then both use it. As a result, the shape logic also gets coverage from the pure-file gate.

review.impact: `MAIN` is exported, but only state.ts uses it. No caller reads the path that `installFakeClaude` returns, at line 43. The module exposes more names than callers need.
review.fix: Remove `export` from `MAIN`. Make `installFakeClaude` return `void`. Do this unless a later ticket needs either one.

review.impact: No test covers two fake calls that start at the same time. `claimRecord` counts the pass from the earlier record files. `readRecord` returns undefined for a record that another call is still writing. That call then drops out of the count. Two parallel builder calls can both get pass=1, and the test chooses the wrong reply. Later tickets will start agent children in parallel, so this case will happen.
review.fix: Add a test in fake-claude.test.ts. Start three `claude` calls with the same role through `Promise.all`. Assert that the passes in `calls()` are exactly [1, 2, 3] and that the record file names are unique. If the test fails, retry `readRecord` until the record parses, or write the role to the file name or to an atomic temporary file that is then renamed.

review.impact: No test covers the `held` path. In that path, a user message arrives on stdin while an ask waits for its `control_response`. The loop then must play the held message as the next turn. If this path breaks, the fake drops or reorders turns, and every test still passes.
review.fix: Add a long-lived test: script an ask on turn 1 and a text reply on turn 2. Send the second user message before the control_response. Assert that `turns` equals both messages in order and that turn 2 gets its result.

review.impact: No test covers `exit` on a reply in a long-lived (`--input-format stream-json`) fake. The script docs say that this ends the process after the turn. If `finish(code)` were removed, the fake would wait for more input, and no test would fail.
review.fix: Add a test. Start a stream-json fake whose turn-1 reply has `exit: 2`. Send one message and keep stdin open. Assert that `child.exited` resolves to 2.

review.impact: No end-to-end test covers `--output-format json`. The test of `parseArgs` checks only the parsing. The branch that prints the result as one JSON line is not run, so a regression there passes.
review.fix: Add a headless test that runs `claude -p hi --output-format json`. Parse stdout as one JSON object and assert `type: 'result'` and the result text.

review.impact: No test covers the guard that stops a run when PATH finds a real `claude`. If the check on the marker text breaks, for example after a rename of the 'fake claude' comment in bin/claude, the guard passes silently. It then no longer protects plain `bun test` runs.
review.fix: Move the check into a function that takes the path of the found file, for example `isFake(path)`, and give it a unit test. The test passes a temporary script without the marker and asserts that the function throws. The test also asserts that src/test/fake-claude/bin/claude passes.

review.impact: Each fake call runs `claimRecord`. It lists the calls folder again on every loop pass, then reads and parses every earlier record to count the pass. With N calls in one test, the total cost is O(N²) file reads. This is small for the current tests, which make a few calls each. A long-lived test with many fake calls, such as a `times`-heavy or multi-pass build loop, pays the cost again on each start.
review.fix: Read the folder list one time before the loop and reuse it. Better: write the role into the file name (for example `0003.builder.json`), so the pass count comes from the file names only, with no `readRecord` calls.

review.impact: The lock does not reliably allow only one server when two servers start at the same moment and the lock file is stale or absent. The sequence is: A and B both read the stale holder; A runs rmSync and writes with 'wx', which succeeds; B then runs rmSync, which deletes A's new lock, and B's 'wx' write also succeeds. Both processes now think they hold the lock and both serve the same log. The 'EEXIST' branch only catches the case where B writes before A's write finishes, so the comment overstates the protection.
review.fix: Do not remove a lock file unless you have checked that it is still the stale file you read. One way: rename the stale file to a unique temp name with renameSync, which fails if another process already moved it, then write with 'wx'. Another way: read the file again just before rmSync, and delete only if it still has the same stale content. Change the comment so it describes the protection that the code really gives.

review.impact: The code replaces `vite.environments.client.hot.send` with its own function and assumes a payload shape (`args[0].type === 'full-reload'`). This depends on Vite internals that are not part of the public API. If Vite sends full reloads through another path or changes the `send` overloads, the `reload` event stops firing and no test or compiler error shows it. The page would then reload through Vite's own socket and lose the composer draft.
review.fix: Use a supported hook if one exists, for example a small Vite plugin with `hotUpdate` that decides when a full reload is needed. If you keep the override, put a comment on it that names the Vite version it was checked against. The reload test already covers the behavior.

review.impact: `run` returns 0 while the server is still running. The process stays alive only because the open handles keep it running, and it later exits from inside `start.ts` through `process.exit(0)` in the signal handler. This breaks the `Verb.run` contract ('Returns the exit code'): any change that makes cli.ts call `process.exit` after `run` returns stops the server at once. Also, SIGINT/SIGTERM always exit with code 0.
review.fix: Make `serve.run` wait until the server closes, for example by giving `LiveServer` a `closed: Promise<void>` that the signal handler resolves, and return the exit code from `run`. Move the `process.exit` call out of `start.ts`.

review.impact: `lock.ts` and `listen.ts:11` each define the same `sleep` helper. The two copies can drift apart.
review.fix: Use `Bun.sleep`, which the rest of the server code already uses, or `setTimeout` from `node:timers/promises`. Then delete both local copies.

review.impact: `waitForUrl` repeats the `werk: serving (http://\S+)` regex and the boot-timeout logic of `spawnServe().serving()` in `src/test/server-harness.ts`. If the start-up message changes, two places must change.

review.impact: `boot` keeps two names for the same object: `let live` holds `server`, and `viteServer` holds `vite`. It also creates `handle: () => {}` as a placeholder and replaces it later. A reader must track all three aliases to see that a request cannot reach the empty handler.
review.fix: Have the HTTP callback call `server.handle` through a single `let server: LiveServer | undefined`. Narrow `vite` with a non-null assertion after the try block, or start Vite before the try block. Then remove the `live` and `viteServer` aliases.

review.impact: `DRAFT_KEY` is exported, but only this module uses it. `clearDraft` does the same work as `stashDraft(storage, '')`, so the module has more public functions than it needs.
review.fix: Stop exporting `DRAFT_KEY`. Remove `clearDraft` and call `stashDraft(sessionStorage, '')` instead, or keep `clearDraft` and have `stashDraft` call it for empty text.

review.impact: The code replaces `hot.send` and uses two `as` casts that remove the type checks. If Vite changes the signature of `send`, the compiler does not report the change.

review.impact: The test 'an edit to a component applies in place and pushes no "reload"' has no positive control. It sleeps 500 ms and asserts that only 'hello' arrived. It also passes when Vite never sees the edit, for example when the watcher is not ready, the file is not in the module graph, or the change detection breaks. So it does not prove that Vite handled the change in place.

Then edit web/main.tsx and assert that the next event is 'reload' and `received()` is ['hello','reload']. The order then shows that the App.tsx edit pushed nothing.

review.impact: No test covers the `else send(...args)` branch. That branch forwards the in-place HMR updates of Vite to the page. review.impact: The handler serves `/api/state` and `/api/live` before the request reaches Vite, so these routes skip Vite's Host-header check (`hostValidationMiddleware`). A web page can use DNS rebinding to point its own hostname at 127.0.0.1:4211. It can then read the server pid, the instance id and the absolute `logPath`, which contains the user's home directory, and it can subscribe to the live channel. The binding to 127.0.0.1 does not block this attack. The risk grows when later tickets put log content and agent control on `/api/`.
review.fix: In `createHandler`, reject every `/api/` request with 403 unless the `Host` header is `127.0.0.1:<port>` or `localhost:<port>`. Alternatively, send all requests through Vite's host validation first. Add a test that sends `Host: evil.example` and expects 403.

review.impact: `readEvents` casts each parsed line to `Event` and does not check it. A line that is valid JSON but has the wrong shape passes through. Examples are a hand-edited line, a line from a future version, or `{"type":"node.proposed"}` with no payload. `fold` then throws a TypeError, such as "Cannot destructure property 'id' of 'e.payload'". `cli.ts` prints this as `werk: Cannot destructure ...`. The message does not name the file or the line, but the JSON error does. An event with an unknown `type` is also dropped with no message.
review.fix: In `readEvents`, check the minimum shape of each line: a numeric `seq`, a known `type`, and an object `payload` with a string `id`. If the check fails, throw the same `${path}:${n} is not a valid event` style of error that the JSON error uses.

review.impact: `appendEvent` reads and parses the whole log again to find the last `seq`. `writeMap` in `src/cli/map-verb.ts` already read and folded the log, so each write parses the log two times. The read-then-append is also not atomic. Two `werk` processes that run at the same time can write the same `seq`, or plan against a stale map. For example, both can propose the same id, and the fold then drops the second proposal with no message.
review.fix: Read the log one time. Let `writeMap` pass the last `seq` it read to `appendEvent`, or let `appendEvent` take the events list. If concurrent agents are in scope, take a lock file around the read-plan-append step, or document that one writer at a time is assumed.

review.impact: The new `try/catch` turns every exception from a verb into a one-line `werk: <message>`. This includes programmer errors such as a TypeError or a ReferenceError. The stack trace is lost, so a bug in a verb is hard to locate.
review.fix: Throw a dedicated error class, for example `WerkError`, from `log.ts` for expected failures (a broken log, a failed write). Catch only that class in `cli.ts` and rethrow other errors. Or print the stack when an env flag such as `WERK_DEBUG` is set.

review.impact: The event schema module imports `QuotePointer` from `transcript.ts`, which is the transcript parser. The persisted log format now depends on a parser module. A change to the parser's types silently changes the shape of the stored events.
review.fix: Move `QuotePointer` and `Speaker` into `events.ts`, or into a small types module. Let `transcript.ts` import them from there.

review.impact: `readTranscript` drops the cause of the error. A missing file, a permission error and a directory path all give the same message: `cannot read the transcript <path>.`. The agent cannot tell which fix to apply.
review.fix: Add the error code or the message to the text, for example `cannot read the transcript ${path}: ${(err as NodeJS.ErrnoException).code}.`.

review.impact: The `record` and `ev` helpers are copied word for word from `src/map/format.test.ts:6-17`. `card` in `src/map/fold.test.ts:13` is a third copy with small differences. If `NodeRecord` or `Event` changes, all three copies need the same edit, and they can drift apart.
review.fix: Move one `record`/`ev` pair into a shared test helper, for example `src/test/map-fixtures.ts`, and import it in the three map test files.

review.impact: The membership check `(X as readonly string[]).includes(v)` appears three times (kinds at line 48, who at line 52, actors at line 131). Lines 81 and 85 then need `kind as NodeRecord['kind']` and `who as NodeRecord['who']` casts. The casts and the checks are separate, so a later edit can remove a check and leave an unchecked cast.
review.fix: Add one type guard, `isOneOf<T extends string>(list: readonly T[], v: string): v is T`, and use it in the three checks. TypeScript then narrows `kind` and `who`, so you can delete the two casts in the payload.

review.impact: `m.nodes.get(id) as never` turns off type checking for the `formatNode` argument in four places. A wrong id or a change to the `MapNode` type then gives no compile error.
review.fix: Use a small helper that throws when the node is missing and returns `MapNode`, for example `const node = (id: string) => m.nodes.get(id) ?? fail(id)`. Or use a non-null assertion. Both keep the parameter type checked.

review.impact: `readTranscript` returns `TranscriptFile | string` and uses a string as the error. The rest of the change uses `{ ok: true } | { ok: false; error }` results (`ParseResult`, `Plan`, `FindResult`). The caller must use `typeof transcript === 'string'`, which is a different pattern for the same idea.
review.fix: Return `{ ok: true; file: TranscriptFile } | { ok: false; error: string }`. Then line 33 can return the failure directly, as the other plan steps do.

review.impact: `readEvents` casts each parsed line to `Event` without checks. The log is a plain file in the project, and people can edit it by hand. A line such as `{"type":"node.proposed","payload":null}` makes `fold` throw `Cannot destructure property 'id' of 'e.payload'`. The error does not name the bad line. A non-numeric `seq` on the last line, for example `"5"`, makes `appendEvent` write `seq: "51"`. That corrupts the numbering for every later event.
review.fix: After `JSON.parse`, check each line: `seq` is a number, `type` is a known `EventType`, `actor` is in `ACTORS`, and `payload` is an object with a string `id`. On a failed check, throw the same `${path}:${n} is not a valid event` error that a JSON error gets.

review.impact: `formatNode` prints title, why, body, parent title and session name unchanged. The body of an excerpt is a copy of transcript text, and the session name can come from the file. Any of these values can hold ANSI or other control characters (ESC, CR). `werk show` then writes those bytes to the terminal. They can rewrite or hide earlier output lines, so the person or the agent can read the wrong status or the wrong `proposed` flag.
review.fix: Before printing, replace C0/C1 control characters other than `\n` and `\t` in each value with a visible escape, for example `\x1b`. Do this in `formatNode`. As an alternative, refuse control characters in `planAdd` and `planEdit`.

review.impact: appendEvent calls readEvents again to get the last seq. writeMap in src/cli/map-verb.ts has already read and parsed the whole log to fold it. So every write verb reads the full log from disk and runs JSON.parse on every line two times. The log is append-only and only grows, so the cost of every add, edit, accept and discard grows with the full history of the project.
review.fix: Let appendEvent take the next seq, or the last event, from the caller. For example, writeMap reads the events one time, folds them, and passes `events.at(-1)?.seq` to appendEvent. Another option: read only the last non-empty line of the file to get the seq.

review.impact: ghostSubtree scans all nodes for each node it finds, and `found.includes` is a linear scan. The cost is O(nodes × subtree × subtree). fold calls it for each node.discarded event, and planDiscard calls it again. So the time to fold a long log with many discards grows faster than linear. ghostChain has the same pattern with `chain.includes`.
review.fix: Build a parent → children index one time per call, or keep one in the fold. Use a Set for the visited ids in ghostSubtree and ghostChain.

The lock wait (5000 ms) and the listen retry (20 x 250 ms) are in src/server/serve-args.ts:19-25. src/verbs/serve.test.ts:37 covers the wait-then-refuse message. The composer draft survives a reload (e2e/serve.spec.ts:12). An src/ edit hot-reloads in the same process (src/server/hot.test.ts:45).

The card says the order of events answers 'what changed after this card was decided'. src/map/fold.ts drops the seq and the order of events, and keeps no 'decided at' position. No function or test answers that question. Staleness and rederive need it later. To fix: record the seq of the latest status.set to 'decided' for each node, and the seq of each later edit, and add a test in src/map/fold.test.ts.

review.impact: The page fetches the view again only on a `changed` event. When the live channel drops and reconnects, for example after a full restart of `werk serve`, `EventSource` reconnects by itself. A log change in the gap does not push `changed` to this page, so the page keeps a stale map and `data-live` shows 'open'.
review.fix: In `onOpen`, also bump `logVersion` (`setLogVersion((v) => v + 1)`). The page then fetches the open card again on every open and reopen of the live channel.

review.impact: The code replaces the `send` method of the Vite client hot channel (`vite.environments.client.hot.send`) to catch `full-reload`. This depends on Vite internals. A Vite update that sends through another path, or that binds `send` at creation, stops the `reload` push without any error. The composer draft is then lost on a full reload.
review.fix: Use a supported hook: a small Vite plugin whose `hotUpdate` hook finds updates that Vite cannot apply in place, or `server.ws`/`hot.on` events. If the patch stays, add a comment that names the Vite version it was checked against.

review.impact: On a second evaluation, `startServer` ignores `opts` without a message: a different `cwd`, `env`, port or `children` has no effect. The routes get a new handler, but `push`, the log watcher and the Vite hook keep the closures from the first evaluation. An edit to `sse.ts` or `start.ts` therefore does not take effect, but the log says 'hot reload'.
review.fix: Write in the doc comment which modules are swapped on a reload (only routes.ts) and which stay. Or call `live.handle`/`push` through functions that are looked up again on each reload. Write a warning when `opts.cwd` differs from the live server.

review.impact: The cleanup in `boot` covers only `startVite` and `listenWithRetry`. If `lock.update`, `Bun.spawn` of a child, or `watch` throws, nothing has registered the `exit` handler yet. The lock file then stays with a live pid, and Vite and the HTTP server stay open.
review.fix: Put the whole start-up after `takeLock` in one try/catch, or register the `exit` cleanup right after the lock is taken. On an error, close the parts that started and release the lock.

review.impact: `fetchView` reads every 404 as 'missing card'. A 404 from an unknown route or from a server that has no `/api/view` (an old server after a partial restart) shows 'No card #… in the map.' and not an error.
review.fix: Make the server return a typed body for a missing card (for example `{ error: 'no-card', id }`). Map only that body to `missing`, and map other 404 responses to `error`.

review.impact: `lock.ts` and `listen.ts` (line 11) each define the same `sleep` helper. The server code under Bun also has `Bun.sleep`, which the test helpers already use. That gives two hand-written copies of one helper.
review.fix: Use `Bun.sleep` in both server modules, or export one `sleep` from a shared module.

review.impact: `SERVE_USAGE` repeats each flag of the `FLAGS` map by hand. If someone adds or renames a flag in `FLAGS` and forgets the usage string, the `werk` verb list shows wrong flags. No test catches this.
review.fix: Build `SERVE_USAGE` from the keys of `FLAGS`, e.g. `` `serve ${Object.keys(FLAGS).map((f) => `[${f} <n>]`).join(' ')}` ``.

review.impact: `KINDS` repeats the literals of the `NodeKind` union by hand. `toNode` also needs the `as NodeKind` cast. `EDGE_TYPES`/`EdgeType` in the same file already use the pattern that derives the type from the array, so the two lists can drift apart.
review.fix: Declare `export const NODE_KINDS = ['card','source','excerpt','option'] as const` and `type NodeKind = (typeof NODE_KINDS)[number]`. Then use a type guard such as `isEdgeType` in place of the cast.

review.impact: `LiveServer.push` is in the public interface, but no code calls it through `LiveServer`. Only the local `push` closure in `start.ts` uses it. The member is dead, and it makes the interface larger than it needs to be.
review.fix: Remove `push` from `LiveServer` and from the object literal in `start.ts`. Add it back when a route needs it.

review.impact: `boot` keeps two names for one object: `live` (a `let` that starts as undefined, used by the request callback) and `server`. It also sets `handle` to a no-op placeholder and then assigns it again. This makes the start-up order harder to follow.
review.fix: Keep one binding. For example, create `httpServer` with `(req, res) => server.handle(req, res)` after `server` is declared, or set `handle: createHandler(...)` in one place, so the `live` variable and the no-op placeholder go away.

review.impact: `waitForUrl` repeats the `/werk: serving (http:\/\/\S+)/` regex and the wait-for-output logic of `src/test/server-harness.ts`. If the start message changes, someone must edit both harnesses.
review.fix: Export the serving-line regex, e.g. `SERVING_LINE`, from one Node-safe module such as `src/test/app-copy.ts` or a new small module, and import it in both harnesses.

review.impact: The test proves that no event arrives with a fixed `Bun.sleep(500)`. The test is slower than it needs to be. On a slow machine, a late `reload` can arrive after 500 ms, so the test can pass when it should fail.
review.fix: After the edit, wait for a positive signal that Vite has processed the change, e.g. fetch `/App.tsx` until the new text is served. Then assert that `received()` holds only `hello`.

review.impact: The test name says close 'ends the live channel', but the test opens no live client and asserts nothing about it. Delete `for (const client of clients) client.end()` from `close()` and this test still passes. An open SSE connection then keeps `httpServer.close()` waiting, and the bug reaches production with no failing test.
review.fix: Open a live client with `openLive(url(live))` before `live.close()`. Then assert that its stream ends, for example with a `closed()` promise on `LiveClient`. Or give close() a timeout and assert that it resolves before the timeout.

review.impact: The negative test sleeps a fixed 500 ms and then asserts that no `reload` came. Nothing shows that Vite processed the edit to App.tsx. On a slow machine a late `reload` arrives after the check, and the test passes without testing anything. The 200 ms sleep in the start.test.ts test 'a change to another file next to the log pushes nothing' has the same weakness.
review.fix: Wait for a positive signal first. For example, poll `fetch(`${url}/App.tsx`)` until the body contains 'No cards here yet.' Then wait a short settle time and assert that the only received event is `hello`.

review.impact: Two guards in `fold()` have no test: `if (ghosts.delete(p.id)) nodes.delete(p.id)` on `change.discarded`, and `if (node) break` on `node.proposed`. Remove either guard and all tests still pass. A `change.discarded` or a `node.proposed` for an id that is already live would then delete or replace a real card.
review.fix: Add one case: `fold([card('a','A'), ev('change.discarded',{id:'a'}), ev('node.proposed',{id:'a',kind:'card',title:'X'})])`. Assert that card `a` is still live and keeps the title 'A'.

review.impact: The parseLog test covers only a blank line and broken JSON. It does not cover valid JSON that is not an event, such as `null`, `42`, or `{}`, or an event with no payload. Remove the `event && typeof event.type === 'string'` check or the `payload ?? {}` default and the test still passes. Then `fold` crashes on `p.id` for a line like `{"type":"x"}`.
review.fix: Add the lines `null`, `42`, `{}` and `{"type":"x"}` to the parseLog input. Assert that the first three are skipped and that the last one has `payload: {}`.

review.impact: `expect(localStorage.length).toBe(0)` passes even without the fixture's `localStorage.clear()` init script, because every Playwright context starts with empty storage. The assertion claims to test the harness but cannot fail.
review.fix: Remove the assertion. Or make it able to fail: set a localStorage item, reload, and assert that the item is still there (this tests the once-per-tab guard), then assert that a new page in a new context starts empty.

review.impact: The handler serves `/api/state`, `/api/view` and `/api/live` before the request reaches `live.vite.middlewares`. Vite checks the Host header in its own middleware (`hostValidationMiddleware`), so these routes skip that check. The server listens on a fixed port, 4211, by default. A hostile web page can use DNS rebinding: it points its own hostname at 127.0.0.1:4211 and then reads responses as same-origin. It can read the full decision log, including verbatim quotes of what the user said (excerpts), the absolute `logPath`, the server pid, and the live event stream.
review.fix: Check the Host header at the top of `createHandler`. Allow only `127.0.0.1:<port>`, `localhost:<port>` and `[::1]:<port>`. Return 403 for any other host. You can also reuse Vite's host check: run all requests through a host-check step before the `/api/` branch. Add a test that sends `Host: evil.example` to `/api/view` and expects a 403.

review.impact: `card.url` comes from the log. The agent writes the log, and it can copy text from untrusted web sources. The page puts this value into `<a href>` with no scheme check. React 19.3 blocks `javascript:` URLs, so script execution is not possible now. But the link can point to any scheme, for example `file:` or a custom protocol handler. The link also has no `target`/`noopener` policy.
review.fix: Show the link only when `new URL(card.url).protocol` is `http:` or `https:`. Otherwise show the URL as plain text. Add `rel="noreferrer noopener"`.

review.impact: Each `edge.added` event does a linear scan of all edges (`edges.some`) to drop duplicates. Each `edge.removed` event does a `findIndex` plus a `splice`. Each `level.moved` event copies the whole edge array. The fold of a log with E edge events is therefore O(E²). The log is append-only and only grows, and the fold runs again on every `/api/view` request. With a few thousand links, each page fetch spends noticeable CPU time on these scans.
review.fix: Keep the edges in a `Map<string, Edge>` keyed by `${from}\0${to}\0${type}`. A Map keeps insertion order, so the output order does not change. `edge.added` becomes `has`/`set` and `edge.removed` becomes `delete`. For `level.moved`, keep a per-node index of `refines` keys, so the code deletes only that node's refines edges and does not rebuild the array.

review.impact: Every `/api/view` request reads, parses and folds the whole log file from the start. Each `changed` event makes every open tab refetch, so one log write costs (number of clients) × (full log read and fold). This cost grows without limit as the append-only log grows.
review.fix: Cache the folded map on the `LiveServer` and key the cache on the log file's size and mtime from `stat`. The log watcher can also clear the cache. Only re-read and re-fold when the file has changed. Then concurrent requests after one `changed` event share one fold.

review.impact: `readEvents` casts each parsed line to `Event` without a check. A line that is valid JSON but has the wrong shape, for example `{"type":"node.proposed"}` with no payload, passes the read. `fold` then throws a `TypeError` such as "undefined is not an object". The catch-all in `cli.ts` prints this as `werk: ...` without a file name or a line number. The agent cannot find the bad line. A valid-JSON line with an unknown `type` is skipped silently.
review.fix: Add a shape check in `readEvents`: a known `type`, an object `payload`, a number `seq`, and an `actor` from `ACTORS`. Throw the same `${path}:${n} is not a valid event` error that the bad-JSON case uses.

review.impact: The new try/catch turns every exception from every verb into a single `werk: <message>` line. This includes programming errors like a `TypeError` in `fold` or `formatNode`. The comment says the catch is for a broken log or a failed write, but it catches all errors, so real bugs lose their stack trace. Errors that are not `Error` instances print `werk: undefined`.
review.fix: Throw a named error class (for example `LogError`) from `readEvents` and `appendEvent`, and catch only that class in `cli.ts` as a user message. Re-throw other errors, or print `err.stack` for them. Use `String(err)` when `err` is not an `Error`.

review.impact: `appendEvent` reads and parses the full log again only to get the last `seq`. `writeMap` already read the log one line earlier in `src/cli/map-verb.ts`, so every write reads the log two times. The two reads also make the seq/plan pair non-atomic: the plan is checked against one read and numbered from another.
review.fix: Have `writeMap` read the events one time, fold them, and pass the last `seq` (or the events) to `appendEvent`. Another option: let `appendEvent` take the next `seq` as an argument.

review.impact: The event schema module imports `QuotePointer` from `transcript.ts`, which is the transcript parser. The stored log format then depends on a parser module. A change to the parser's types silently changes the persisted event shape.
review.fix: Move `QuotePointer` and `Speaker` into `events.ts`. Let `transcript.ts` import them from `events.ts`.

review.impact: `readTranscript` returns `TranscriptFile | string` and uses a bare string as the error. Every other fallible function in this change uses an `{ ok: false, error }` union (`ParseResult`, `Plan`, `FindResult`). The caller must use `typeof === 'string'` to tell the two cases apart, so error handling is not the same across the map modules.
review.fix: Return `{ ok: true, file } | { ok: false, error }`, the same shape as `FindResult`.

review.impact: `linkLines` uses `e.why === undefined` to separate the parent edges from the typed links. This depends on a fold detail that the `Edge` type does not enforce. A parent edge that gets a `why`, or a typed link with no `why`, prints in the wrong place with no warning.
review.fix: Add an explicit discriminator to `Edge` in `fold.ts`, for example `origin: 'parent' | 'link'`. Filter on that field in `format.ts`.

review.impact: The same membership check, `(X as readonly string[]).includes(v)`, appears four times (kind, who, actor, edge type). Then `as NodeRecord['kind']`, `as NodeRecord['who']` and `as EdgeType` casts narrow the value again. The casts are not tied to the check, so a later edit can drop the check and the cast still compiles.
review.fix: Add one type guard, `const oneOf = <T extends string>(list: readonly T[], v: string): v is T => (list as readonly string[]).includes(v)`. Use it at the four checks and delete the `as` casts in `planAdd` and `planLink`.

review.impact: The `record` and `ev` helpers are copied in `format.test.ts` and `rules.test.ts`. `fold.test.ts` has a near copy (`card`, `log`). A change to `NodeRecord` or `Event` needs three edits.
review.fix: Move one `record`/`ev` (or `card`/`log`) pair to a shared test helper, for example `src/map/test-events.ts`. Import it in the three test files.

review.impact: `m.nodes.get(id) as never` is a type escape hatch, used about ten times. It hides a possibly undefined node from the type checker. If the id is wrong, `formatNode` gets `undefined` and fails with a TypeError, not with a clear assertion.
review.fix: Add one helper `const node = (m: MapState, id: string) => { const n = m.nodes.get(id); if (!n) throw new Error(`no #${id}`); return n }`. Use it in place of `as never`.

review.impact: `MapNode` copies every field of `NodeRecord` by hand (id, kind, title, why, body, who, parent, quote). The fold also copies them one by one. A new field on `NodeRecord` needs an edit in both places, and the fold drops the field without an error if the edit is missed.
review.fix: Declare `type MapNode = Omit<NodeRecord, 'status'> & { status: Status; proposed: boolean }`. In the fold, build the node with a spread: `{ ...e.payload, status: status ?? 'open', proposed: ... }`.

review.impact: `MapArgs` has both `id` and `ids`, and `id` is always `ids[0]`. The two fields hold the same data, and readers must check which one each verb uses.
review.fix: Keep only `ids`. Let single-id verbs destructure `{ ids: [id] }`, as `link` already does with `{ ids: [from, to] }`.

review.impact: The tests 'an edit with two ids exits non-zero' (line 199) and 'a discard with two ids exits non-zero' (line 287) run on an empty map. `#a` is not in the map, so `edit a b` and `discard a b` exit 1 for that reason alone. Both tests pass even if `parseMapArgs` stops refusing extra ids. They do not guard the one-id rule.
review.fix: Make `a` exist first: call `realRoot('a')` for edit and `add('a')` for discard. Then assert that stderr contains 'edit takes one id.' or 'discard takes one id.', and that the log did not change.

review.impact: `show a --x y` runs on an empty map. It exits non-zero because `#a` is not in the map, not because of the unknown flag. The flag check of `show` has no test that fails without it. `show` with no id has the same problem, because the test does not check the message.
review.fix: Add `a` first. Assert that stderr contains 'unknown flag --x' for the flag case and 'show needs an id.' for the no-id case.

review.impact: 'an add with the id of a real card exits non-zero' (line 156) and 'an add with two ids exits non-zero' (line 177) check only the exit code. They do not check stderr or that the log stayed the same. A refusal that still appends an event, or that fails for an unrelated reason, passes.
review.fix: Capture `logText()` before the call and assert that it is the same after. Assert the message: 'is already in the map. To change its words, edit it.' and 'add takes one id.'

review.impact: The `ghostChain` doc says the first step from an option is the card it is an alternative to. No test accepts a ghost option under a ghost card. A change that stops the walk at an option would leave the option real under a ghost parent, and its `alternative_to` edge would stay a ghost edge. No test catches this.
review.fix: Add a fold test: a real root, a proposed card `p` under root, and a proposed option `o` with parent `p`. Accept `o`. Assert that `p` and `o` are both not proposed, and that `edges` contains `{from:'o', to:'p', type:'alternative_to'}`.

review.impact: `readEvents` casts each parsed line to `Event` and does not check its shape. If a hand-edited or damaged log has a line that is valid JSON but not an event (for example `null`, `[]`, or a `node.proposed` with no `payload`), `fold` throws a TypeError such as "Cannot read properties of null". The verb then exits with a message that names neither the file nor the line. A line with an unknown `type` is skipped with no error. The parse error names the file and the line, but this case does not.
review.fix: After `JSON.parse`, check that the value is an object with a numeric `seq`, a known `type` from `EventPayloads`, and an object `payload`. If the check fails, throw `${path}:${i + 1} is not a werk event` in the same way as the JSON error.

review.impact: `planAdd` and `planEdit` only check that `title`, `why` and `body` are not empty. A value can contain a newline, so a title such as `"X\nproposed: no"` makes `formatNode` print a line that looks like a real field. The `werk show` output then tells the agent that a ghost is accepted. The log stores the true state, but the text form is the agent's view of the map.
review.fix: Refuse a newline in `title` and `why` in `planAdd` and `planEdit`. Or, in `formatNode`, escape a newline in each single-line field, for example with `JSON.stringify`, or print the value indented. `body` is already printed after a blank line, so it can keep its newlines.

review.impact: `--transcript` accepts any path, resolved against cwd, and any readable file passes as long as one line parses as a `{message:{role,content}}` object. The agent can write a file that contains the quote and then cite it. The "never written from memory" rule then depends on trust in the agent, not on the session store. The session name also comes from the file name, so the agent controls it.
review.fix: Resolve the transcript only inside the Claude Code session directory (`~/.claude/projects/<encoded-cwd>/`), or refuse a path outside it. Take the session from the `sessionId` of the message, and refuse the excerpt when the message has none, instead of using `basename(path)`.

review.impact: `appendEvent` reads the whole log and runs `JSON.parse` on every line only to find the last `seq`. `writeMap` (src/cli/map-verb.ts:59) has already read and parsed the same file for the fold. So every write verb reads and parses the full log two times. The log only grows, so each `add`, `accept`, `edit`, `link` and `discard` gets slower as the project history grows.
review.fix: Read the events one time in `writeMap`. Pass the next `seq` (the last event's `seq` + 1) or the events into `appendEvent`. Another option: in `appendEvent`, parse only the last non-empty line of the file.

review.impact: For each `edge.linked` event, the fold does a linear `links.some` scan to find a duplicate. A full fold is therefore O(L²) in the number of links, and every CLI call runs a full fold.
review.fix: Keep a `Set` of `${from}\u0000${to}\u0000${type}` keys next to `links`. Remove the keys of dropped links in `node.discarded`, or rebuild the set after the filter.

review.impact: `ghostSubtree` scans every node for each found id and calls `found.includes` each time. The cost is O(n·k²) for a subtree of k ghosts in a map of n nodes. A discard during the fold and `planDiscard` both call it.
review.fix: Build a parent→children index one time, or use a `Set` for `found`. Then do a breadth-first walk over the children of each found id.

causeOfLast.why: pass 1 added the pure modules without putting them on the pure-file list, against the rule in that file, and did not add the remove and restore events that `#pr-log` and `#werk-write` name.

grade.gap: v0 includes 'the CLI as the only write path, with remove and find'. The diff adds remove and restore (src/verbs/remove.ts, src/verbs/restore.ts), but it has no find verb. No src/verbs/find.ts exists, and no test in src/map/map.cli.test.ts lists the open cards. Add a find verb that lists open cards from the fold, and add a CLI test for it. The diff does not touch the chat, the board, the dev loop or the browser views. Other tickets cover them.

The CLI seam tests in src/map/map.cli.test.ts cover add, decide, amend, remove and restore, accept, discard, reopen, confirm and quote. No CLI test covers a note: say writes a note and a thread is read back. commands.test.ts tests the 'note' op only as a pure function. Add a map.cli.test.ts case that runs `say` and then `show`, and check that the note is in the output.

This diff adds no chat code. The note half of the card is present: the say verb appends note.added, and the fold collects notes on the card. The server note route and the clipboard copy are not in the diff.

This diff has no map ✓ control, so the accept path exists only on the command line. The ghost-node rendering (grey or dashed) is also not in the diff. Both belong to the browser ticket. The CLI and fold rules are in place: frozen words, held edges, auto-accept of ancestors, cascade discard, and the --actor you speed bump.
The card lists 'find open cards: #werk-find' under Reading. The diff registers no find verb, so `werk help` does not print it. Add src/verbs/find.ts.

The card says an option has one link only: alternative_to. The link command in src/map/commands.ts link() does not refuse a refines link from an option card. Refuse any link from a kind=option node except alternative_to, and add a test in commands.test.ts.

review.impact: `write()` checks the command against one read of the log. Then `appendEvents` reads the log a second time to get the next seq, and it appends with no lock. The header comment says the CLI and the page both call `runCommand`. If two writers run at the same time, one writer can append events that it validated against an old log. Both writers can also take the same seq numbers. This can break the guarantees of the contract check, of #map-frozen and of the ghost rules.
review.fix: Put the read, the `runCommand` call and the append in one function in `src/map/log.ts`, for example `commit(path, (log) => Result)`, and run it under a file lock. Compute the seq from the log that the command was checked against, so the log is read one time only.

review.impact: `readLog` calls `JSON.parse` on each line and does not catch errors. A torn last line from an interrupted append, or a line edited by hand, makes every verb (`map`, `show`, every write) crash with a raw stack trace. The output does not name the file or the line number.
review.fix: Catch the parse error and throw, or return, an error that names the log path and the line number. Optionally, skip an incomplete last line that has no newline. Let the CLI print that message and exit 1.

review.impact: `runCommand` is the one write path for the CLI and the page, and it validates every other enum itself (kind, status, who, edge type, reason). It does not validate `criterion.form`: only `src/verbs/kill.ts` checks it against `FORMS`. A caller from the page can write a `kill.added` event with any form. The list of forms also exists in two places: `FORMS` in `src/verbs/kill.ts` and the error text in `commands.ts`.
review.fix: Move `KILL_FORMS` to `events.ts`, type `KillCriterion.form` with it, and validate the form in the `kill` case of `plan()`. Then let `src/verbs/kill.ts` only parse the flags.

review.impact: `flag()` and `has()` treat `--a_b` and `--a-b` as the same flag, but `all()` does not. A repeated flag spelled with the other separator is lost without a message. This contradicts the module's doc comment.
review.fix: Normalize the name when `parseArgs` stores it, for example map `_` to `-`. Then make `flag`, `has` and `all` all look up the normalized key.

review.impact: `quote` does not use `writeVerb`. It reports a bad `--actor` value as a generic usage error and does not print the message 'werk: --actor must be you or agent.' that the other write verbs print. `show.ts:20` also copies the 'no card' text of `known()`, and it says that a removed card is unknown instead of telling the user to restore it.
review.fix: Reuse the actor check from `write.ts` (export a helper that returns the error text). In `show`, use the same message as `commands.ts` for a removed card, for example by exporting `known()` or a `describeMissing(g, id)` helper.

review.impact: `all()` does not apply the `_`/`-` alias that `flag()` applies. `all(a, 'why_not')` returns `[]` when the user typed `--why-not`, but `flag(a, 'why_not')` returns the value. No verb calls `all()`; only the test calls it. So it is dead code, and it is also easy to use in the wrong way.
review.fix: Delete `all()` and its test until a verb needs it. Or put the alias lookup into one helper that `flag()` and `all()` both call.

review.impact: Nothing in `src` calls `appendMessage`, and no test covers it. It is dead code in the diff, and it also writes a second form of the transcript row shape that `parseTranscript` must keep in sync with.
review.fix: Remove `appendMessage` until the chat pane that writes transcripts is part of a change.

review.impact: `werk add` accepts `--obligation`, and it is in `Command`, `EventBody` and the usage text. `fold` never reads it, and `MapNode` has no `obligation` field. The flag writes data that no code uses, so readers think the flag works.
review.fix: Remove `obligation` from the add verb, the `add` command, `pick` and `EventBody`. Or fold it into `MapNode` and read it where it matters.

review.impact: The two lines `const err = known(g, id); if (err) return fail(err)` appear in about twelve branches of `plan` and its helpers. A new command can leave out the check without any warning.
review.fix: Add a helper, for example `const unknown = (g, id) => { const e = known(g, id); return e ? fail(e) : undefined }`. Or check `known` once in `plan` for every op that has an `id` (all ops except `restore`), and remove the copies.

review.impact: `show` copies the text `no card "…" in the map. Run \`werk map\`…` from `known()` in commands.ts. `show` does not report the removed-card case that `known()` reports. The two messages will drift apart.
review.fix: Export `known()` from commands.ts, or move it to a shared module, and call it from `show`.

review.impact: The kill forms are written three times: `FORMS` in the verb, the error text in `plan` 'kill' (`metric|manual|no-metric|revisit`), and the fix text in contract.ts. A new form needs three edits.
review.fix: Export `KILL_FORMS` from events.ts next to `STATUSES`. Build the error text and the usage text from it.

review.impact: The `--who` check (`cmd.who === undefined ? undefined : oneOf(...)` and the same error) is copied in `add` and `edit`. The optional-`--status` check in `add` has the same shape.
review.fix: Add `optionalOneOf(value, allowed, flagName)`. It returns the parsed value or a refusal. Use it for `who` and `status`.

review.impact: `quote` writes its own copy of the `writeVerb` flow (parse, `actorOf`, error, `write`). A bad `--actor` prints only the generic usage line. `writeVerb` prints `--actor must be you or agent`.
review.fix: Use the same actor error as `writeVerb`. Or give `writeVerb` an async or side-input `build` hook so that `quote` can reuse it.

review.impact: `as never` hides the `undefined` result of `find`. If the fixture changes and no edge matches, `isLive` crashes with a TypeError, not a clear assertion failure.
review.fix: Assign the edge to a variable. Assert `expect(edge).toBeDefined()`, then pass `edge!` or narrow it with a guard.

review.impact: Only one case tests the #map-frozen guard: `kill --clear` on a decided card. Nothing tests `unlink` of the only depends_on link, `edit --basis` (noBasis null), or `edit --who you` on a decided card. If `touched()` returned `cmd.to` for link/unlink, or `guardFrozen` skipped `edit`, a decided card could silently lose its basis or its options, and every test would still pass.
review.fix: Add refusal cases to this test. Use `decidedCard('a')` plus a depends_on link a->b, then run `unlink a b --type depends_on`. Run `{op:'edit', id:'a', noBasis:null}` on `decidedCard('a')`. Run `{op:'edit', id:'a', who:'you'}`. Expect 'would remove a required fact' for each. Also check that `status`/`reopen` on a decided card do not hit the guard.

review.impact: No test covers the two refusal paths of `writeVerb`. One path rejects a bad `--actor` value, for example `--actor You`. The other prints usage when `build` returns an error string, for example `werk kill` with no id. If the actor check fell back to 'agent' or the exit code changed, no test would fail. The accept guard depends on `--actor` being parsed strictly.
review.fix: In map.cli.test.ts, add a test that runs `werk accept g --actor You` and `werk kill` with no id. For each, expect code 1, stderr that contains `--actor must be you or agent` or `usage: werk kill`, and an unchanged log.

review.impact: The test title says the link comes back 'in any order', but the test restores only in the order a then b. A fold bug that restores waiting links only when the second end restored is the `to` end would pass.
review.fix: Add the reverse order: restore b, then a, and expect `edges` to have length 1.

review.impact: The test title says 'a second restore changes nothing', but the test restores only an unknown id. It never restores a real card twice, so a double `node.restored` that duplicates edges or resets fields is not tested.
review.fix: Add a remove of a real card, then two `node.restored` events. Expect one node, `removed.size` 0, and no duplicate edges.

review.impact: `flag()` treats `_` and `-` as the same flag, but `all()` does not. The test checks `all` only with a name that has neither character, so the mismatch is not tested. Today a future caller of `all(a, 'min_sample')` gets [] for `--min-sample`.
review.fix: Make `all()` use the same alias lookup as `flag()`, and add an assertion such as `all(parseArgs(['--a-b','1']), 'a_b')` equals ['1']. Or delete `all()`, because no code calls it.

review.impact: `appendMessage` puts `session` into `join(dir, `${session}.jsonl`)` without a check. The header comment says the chat pane writes transcripts through this function. If a later caller passes a session id from a request (for example, a browser control), a value such as `../../x` writes a `.jsonl` file outside `.werk/transcripts`. This is path traversal. No code calls the function yet.
review.fix: Check the session id before the join. Use a strict pattern such as `/^[A-Za-z0-9._-]+$/` with no `..`, or check that `resolve(dir, file)` starts with `resolve(dir) + sep`. Refuse every other value.

review.impact: `resolveSession` joins `name` into `transcriptsDir(store)` with no check, and the fallback accepts any existing path that ends in `.jsonl`. `werk quote <card> ../../some/file` reads a file outside the store, and the quoted text goes into the log. The CLI user already has file access, so the risk is low today. If the page controls later pass the session name through this function, it becomes an arbitrary file read.
review.fix: For the id and prefix lookups, refuse a `name` that contains `/`, `\` or `..`. Keep the explicit-path fallback only for the command line, and make it a separate, named option. Do not let it run on an id lookup.

review.impact: deriveMarks scans every live edge once for each change. Each body/why edit and each retitle of a real card adds a change, and the list never shrinks. The cost is O(changes × edges), and it grows without limit as the log grows. Every CLI read runs fold once, and every write runs it twice. With a long-lived log, for example 10k amends and 2k edges, that is about 20M edge checks per fold. The postponement BFS also rescans all live edges for each dequeued node, which is O(V × E) for each postponement.
review.fix: Build the live edges once into a Map keyed by `to`, holding only depends_on and refines edges. For each change, look up only the edges into c.id. The postponement BFS can use the same index for depends_on edges.

review.impact: formatStale calls the recursive `depth()` inside the sort comparator, with no memo. Each call scans all of g.edges and calls ids.includes, which is O(marks). Sort makes O(m log m) comparisons, so the total is about O(m log m × E × m). A large stale cascade, such as a reopen above hundreds of dependent cards, makes `werk stale` slow.
review.fix: Make a Set from `ids`. Compute depth once per marked id into a Map, with a memo, before the sort. Then sort by the cached values.

review.impact: One write reads and parses the whole log two times: once in write(), and again inside appendEvents to find the last seq. It also folds the whole log two times: once in runCommand, and again in guardFrozen, which re-folds log plus the new events. Every write costs about 2× read+parse and 2× fold, so cost grows linearly with log size, twice.
review.fix: Pass the last seq (log.at(-1)?.seq) from the log that write() already read into appendEvents, for example as an optional parameter. In guardFrozen, run the second fold only when a touched id is decided in g. Check that before you build `after`.

review.impact: deriveRollup runs a full subtree walk from every card, so a deep refines chain costs O(V × depth), about O(V²). The kids map is built with `[...(kids.get(e.to) ?? []), e.from]`, which copies the array on every push, so it is O(k²) for each parent. addEdge also does a linear edges.find for each edge.added event, which is O(E²) over the log.
review.fix: Compute the rollups bottom-up in one post-order pass, with a memo for each child's rollup, and push into the kids arrays in place. Keep a Set of edge keys (`from|to|type`) next to `edges` so the duplicate check in addEdge is O(1).

review.impact: This file is an executable script. On load, it reads the environment, writes files and calls process.exit. It also exports the shared types FakeStep and FakeScript, and harness.ts imports them. Only the `import type` in harness.ts stops the script from running. If a later edit changes this to a value import, or adds a runtime export, then loading the harness runs the fake agent inside the test process, and the agent calls process.exit(64) there.
review.fix: Move FakeStep and FakeScript to a module that has no side effects, for example src/test/fake-script.ts. Import the types from that module in both fake-agent.ts and harness.ts. Keep fake-agent.ts as a pure entry point that exports nothing.

review.impact: JSON.parse and readFileSync can throw on a missing script or bad JSON. The error is not caught, so Bun prints a stack trace and exits 1. The other script errors use the `fake agent:` prefix and exit 64. A test that checks the exit code or stderr cannot tell this error from a scripted `exit: 1`. Also, the WERK_FAKE_AGENT_SCRIPT check at line 27 does not use the `fail` helper and repeats its logic, because `fail` is declared after that check.
review.fix: Declare `fail` first, and use it for the missing-env check. Put the read and the parse in a try/catch that calls fail(64, `cannot read the script: ...`).

review.impact: The entry point handles no errors. Two errors print a raw stack trace, and the clean `werk: ...` message is lost in it: a verb that throws in run, and registry.register throwing at import time for a duplicate or invalid name. dispatch returns exit codes on purpose (2 for an unknown verb). A thrown error goes around that contract and exits 1 with stack noise.
review.fix: Put loadVerbs and dispatch in a try/catch in main.ts. Write `werk: <message>` to stderr and exit with a defined code, for example 1. Alternatively, catch the error in dispatch and send it through io.err.

review.impact: judge and gateReport each take their own `threshold` parameter, and each defaults to THRESHOLD. A caller can pass a custom threshold to judge and forget to pass it to gateReport. Then the report header and the summary line state a different percentage from the one that set each `ok`.
review.fix: Pass the threshold one time. For example, have judge return { threshold, verdicts }, or store the threshold on each FileVerdict. Then gateReport reads the threshold from its input and has no threshold parameter.

review.impact: dispatch receives the registry as a parameter, but a verb gets only (args, io). The help verb therefore reads the module-level `registry` singleton directly. If dispatch runs with a different registry, help lists the wrong verbs. This makes the dependency injection in dispatch inconsistent, and help can only be tested through the global registry.
review.fix: Pass a context to Verb.run that contains the registry, for example run(args, io, { registry }). Alternatively, make Io carry the registry. Then help reads the registry that dispatch got.

review.impact: The file writes the edit-step shape `{ edit: { path: string; content: string } }` three times: in `FakeStep`, in the `isEdit` guard, and in the cast on line 52. The guard does not narrow `step`, because `fail` is a const arrow function with no explicit `never` assertion signature. So the code needs the manual cast `(step as {...})`, and later `exit as number`. If someone changes the step shape in one place only, the cast hides the mismatch and typecheck still passes.
review.fix: Declare `type EditStep = Extract<FakeStep, { edit: unknown }>` and use it in `isEdit`. Declare `fail` as `function fail(code: number, message: string): never` so control flow narrows after `if (!isEdit(step)) fail(...)` and after the `exit` check. Then delete the `as { edit: ... }` and `as number` casts.

review.impact: The missing-script check writes to stderr and calls `process.exit(64)` by hand, and it does this before `fail` exists. Two code paths now do the same job. A change to the error format reaches only one of them.
review.fix: Move the `fail` declaration above the first check and write `if (!scriptPath) fail(64, 'WERK_FAKE_AGENT_SCRIPT is not set')`.

review.impact: The test uses its own rule to find verb files: `!f.includes('.test.')`. `load-verbs.ts` uses a different rule, `isVerbModule`, which also excludes `.spec.` files and non-TS files. The two copies can drift apart, and the test can then check a different set of verbs than the CLI loads.
review.fix: Export `isVerbModule` (or a `listVerbFiles(dir)` helper) from `src/cli/load-verbs.ts`. Use it in the test, and use `VERBS_DIR` in place of `join(SRC, 'cli', 'verbs')`.

review.impact: The local `run` helper repeats the spawn-and-collect code from `harness.ts` (`Bun.spawnSync` with piped stdout and stderr, then a map to `{ code, stdout, stderr }`). `gate-cli.test.ts` repeats the same code a third time. A change to `RunResult`, such as the `?? -1` exit-code default, reaches only one copy.
review.fix: Export a `spawn(cmd: string[], opts?)` helper that returns `RunResult` from `src/test/harness.ts`. Use it in `harness.ts`, `cli.test.ts` and `gate-cli.test.ts`.

review.impact: The help verb registers the name with the literal `'help'`, but `dispatch.ts` sends empty argv to `DEFAULT_VERB`. If someone renames one of them and not the other, `werk` with no arguments exits 2 with an unknown-verb error.
review.fix: Import `DEFAULT_VERB` from `../dispatch.ts` and use it as the name in `help.ts`. Or move the constant next to the help verb and import it in `dispatch.ts`.

review.impact: Three failure paths in the fake agent have no test: `WERK_FAKE_AGENT_SCRIPT` is not set (exit 64), the script has no `steps` array (exit 64), and `exit` is not a number (exit 64). If someone breaks a guard, a bad script can run with no steps and exit 0. A later build test that depends on the fake agent then passes for the wrong reason.
review.fix: In `src/test/harness.test.ts`, add one test for each path. Write `{}` as the script, then `{ steps: [], exit: 'x' }`. For the third case, run `claude` with `WERK_FAKE_AGENT_SCRIPT` removed from the environment. Assert exit code 64 and the stderr message each time.

review.impact: The missing-report test only checks that stderr contains `'no '`. Many unrelated errors contain that text, for example a Bun stack trace such as 'no such file'. A gate that crashes on a missing file instead of printing its own message still passes the test.
review.fix: Assert the full message: `expect(p.stderr.toString()).toContain(`coverage gate: no ${join(dir, 'none.info')}. Run:`)`.

review.impact: The test name says werk runs in the project directory, but the test only checks exit 0 and that stdout contains 'help'. The test still passes if `werk` runs with a different working directory.
review.fix: Assert the working directory. Example: compare `p.run(['pwd'])` with `realpathSync(p.dir)`, or check a later verb that reads the cwd. Otherwise rename the test to 'werk help runs through the harness'.

review.impact: No test covers a fraction just below the threshold that rounds up, for example 8995/10000 = 89.95%. The gate correctly fails it, but the report prints `FAIL   90.0%`. That line confuses the reader, and no test fixes the intended output.
review.fix: Add a case `judge(report({ 'a.ts': [8995, 10000] }), ['a.ts'])` that asserts `ok` is false. Also assert the printed line. If the gate must not print '90.0%' for a failed file, change the format to floor the value or to print two decimals.

review.impact: The shim script puts the Bun path and the fake-agent path in POSIX `sh` double quotes with `JSON.stringify`. In `sh`, double quotes still expand `$`, a backtick and `\`, and `JSON.stringify` escapes none of them. A checkout or Bun install path that contains one of these characters makes `sh` expand or run that text each time a test starts the fake agent. The result is a broken harness or a command that the path chose. The risk is small because the developer controls both paths.
