review.impact: readBoardLog only checks that a line is valid JSON, then casts it straight to BoardEvent. A line that parses to something other than an event object, such as `null`, `42` or `[]`, makes foldBoard throw at `event.type`. A planned payload whose blocked_by is not an array passes refusal(), then makes openBlockers throw on `.filter` at the next move to building. Either way the whole fold throws, so `ticket list` and every write fail with a raw TypeError. That breaks the stated design that one bad line, say from a merge, must not hide the rest of the board.
review.fix: In readBoardLog, check each parsed line's shape: an object with a numeric seq and a string type. Put any line that fails in `unreadable` with a reason such as 'not a board event'. In refusal(), also check the fields that each event type relies on: `blocked_by` is a string array and `title` is a string for planned, and `to` is a Column for moved. Set the event aside when they are wrong, so apply() and the rules never see a malformed payload.

review.impact: appendBoardEvent reads and folds the log, checks the event, then appends, with no lock or exclusive append. The CLI, the build loop and the merge queue all write to this log. Two writers that overlap can both pass the check against the same stale board and give out the same seq. The second event may then break a rule. The fold sets it aside later, but the writer was already told `ok: true`, and duplicate seqs make the set-aside reports, which name events by seq, ambiguous.
review.fix: Make the read-check-append step exclusive. For example, take a lock file next to board.jsonl (open with O_EXCL, retry and remove it afterwards), or reuse whatever lock the decision log uses (#werk-onelock), and do the read, tryApply and append inside it.

review.impact: A move reads and folds the board log three times: in refuseAgentMove(readBoard), inside appendBoardEvent, and again for the success message. That is extra I/O, and the agent-move check runs against a different snapshot from the one the write is checked against, which widens the race window.
review.fix: Pass the agent-move check into the append as an extra check on the same folded board, e.g. an optional `extraRefusal(board)` parameter on appendBoardEvent. Build the success message from the returned event and the board the append already folded, or have appendBoardEvent return that board, rather than calling readBoard again.

review.impact: The left-to-right column order is now written out in three places: the Column type in events.ts, the MOVES keys in rules.ts, and COLUMNS here. Adding or reordering a column means editing all three, and a column missing from COLUMNS would silently drop its tickets from `ticket list`.
review.fix: Export one `COLUMNS = [...] as const` from events.ts, derive `Column` from it (`(typeof COLUMNS)[number]`), and import it in format.ts. It can also be used to check `to` when the fold validates a moved event.

review.impact: The five columns are spelled out three times: the `Column` union in events.ts, `COLUMNS` here, and the keys of `MOVES` in rules.ts. If a column is added or renamed, these places can drift apart, and `werk ticket list` would silently leave the new column out.
review.fix: In events.ts, export `const COLUMNS = ["blocked", "ready", "building", "merging", "done"] as const` and derive `type Column = (typeof COLUMNS)[number]`. Import `COLUMNS` in format.ts instead of redeclaring it.

review.impact: `refuseAgentMove` repeats `refusePlan` almost line for line: look up the column, allow a missing ticket or an `OPEN` column, otherwise build an "is <column>; ... only a ready or blocked ticket" message. A change to the open-column rule has to be made in both places.
review.fix: Pull out a helper such as `refuseUnlessOpen(board, id, what: string)` that both functions call, or have one function delegate to the other with its own message suffix.

review.impact: The shape `{ line: number; reason: string }` is written out three times: `Board.unreadable`, the `foldBoard` parameter at line 84, and `BoardLog.unreadable` in log.ts. These copies can drift apart.
review.fix: Export a named type, for example `type Unreadable = { line: number; reason: string }`, and use it in all three places.

review.impact: `apply` runs only after `refusal` has confirmed that the ticket exists, so the `ticket === undefined` / `ticket !== undefined` checks in the moved, archived and restored branches can never be true. They are dead defensive branches that hide the invariant.
review.fix: Either make `apply` take the looked-up ticket from `tryApply`, or state the invariant once (for example `const ticket = board.tickets.get(id) as Ticket` in the non-planned branches) and drop the repeated guards.

review.impact: `b.tickets.get("s/02") as never` is a type escape hatch: it switches off type checking for that argument, so the test would still compile if `openBlockers`' signature changed.
review.fix: Use a checked non-null form, such as `b.tickets.get("s/02") as Ticket` after importing the `Ticket` type, or `b.tickets.get("s/02")!` if the lint rules allow it.

review.impact: The helper that builds a test board from events is copied with small differences into format.test.ts, rules.test.ts (`board`) and fold.test.ts (`log`), and each file has its own `planned` helper. A change to the event shape means updating every copy.
review.fix: Move one `boardEvents(...)` / `planned(...)` helper into a shared test module, for example src/board/test-events.ts, and import it in all three test files.

review.impact: A successful write reads and folds the whole board log three times: in `refuseAgentMove`, inside `appendBoardEvent`, and again here just to print the column. The call is also hard to follow, because the success message depends on a fresh read rather than on what was written.
review.fix: Have `appendBoardEvent` return the board after the event is applied (it already folds it for `tryApply`), and print the column from that board instead of calling `readBoard` again.

review.impact: The only bad-line test uses text that fails JSON.parse. Lines that parse as JSON but are not events are never tested, and they crash the fold. The line `null` passes readBoardLog, and then foldBoard throws on `event.type` (src/board/fold.ts:90). A `ticket.planned` line with an id but no `blocked_by` array also gets onto the board, and a later move to building then throws in openBlockers (`ticket.blocked_by.filter`). In both cases `werk ticket list` and every write crash. That breaks the rule stated in log.ts that one bad line must not hide the rest of the board.
review.fix: Add tests with lines such as `null`, `42` and `{"seq":1,"type":"ticket.planned","payload":{"id":"s/01"}}` followed by a move to building. Assert that each one is set aside or listed as unreadable and that the lines after it still fold. Then make readBoardLog or the fold's refusal check that the event is an object and that the payload has the fields it needs (title is a string, blocked_by is an array of strings, `to` is a column).

review.impact: No test checks that a move without a reason clears the reason left by an earlier move (fold.ts sets `ticket.reason = event.payload.reason`). If that line changed to keep the old reason, every test would still pass. A ticket moved from blocked back to ready would then still show the old blocked reason in `werk ticket list`.
review.fix: Add a fold test: move a ticket to blocked with a reason, then to ready without one, and assert that `reason` is undefined. Optionally also assert that the list row has no note.

review.impact: `--actor you` is checked only on restore. Nothing checks that move and archive pass the actor through to appendBoardEvent. If either call dropped the `actor` argument, the event would silently record 'agent' and no test would fail.
review.fix: Add an assertion that `werk ticket move ... --actor you` and `werk ticket archive ... --actor you` each append an event with `actor: "you"`.

review.impact: readBoardLog casts each parsed line to BoardEvent without checking it. A line that is valid JSON but not an object, such as `null`, `42` or `"x"`, gets through. foldBoard (fold.ts:90) then throws on `event.type`. One such line makes `werk ticket list` crash and makes every `appendBoardEvent` call fail. This defeats the stated aim that one bad line must not hide the rest of the board. A line whose `seq` is not a number, such as `"seq":"x"`, makes the next append compute `"x" + 1` = `"x1"`. That corrupts every seq written after it.
review.fix: After JSON.parse, check that the value is a non-null object with a finite integer `seq` and a string `type`. Otherwise push it to `unreadable` with a reason such as `not a board event`, the same way a JSON parse error is handled. When computing the next seq, use the largest valid numeric seq, not `events.at(-1)?.seq`.

review.impact: refusal() checks only that `payload.id` is a string. A `ticket.planned` event whose `blocked_by` is not an array, or whose `title` is not a string, is still applied to the board. The bad value then breaks later code: `openBlockers` calls `ticket.blocked_by.filter`, which throws when a later move to building is checked. That move check runs in both the fold and `appendBoardEvent`, so one malformed plan line crashes `werk ticket list` and every later write. A hand-edited or badly merged board log is enough to cause it, and the fold is meant to set such an event aside.
review.fix: Check the payload shape for each event type in refusal(): for ticket.planned, `title` must be a string and `blocked_by` an array of strings; for ticket.moved, `to` must be one of the five columns and `reason` a string or absent. Return a set-aside reason such as `a ticket.planned event has a malformed payload` when the check fails.

review.impact: Ticket ids, titles and reasons from the board log, and from the `--reason` flag, are printed to the terminal as they are. If they contain ANSI escape sequences or control characters, they can rewrite or hide lines in the terminal output of `werk ticket list`.
review.fix: Before printing, strip or escape control characters (C0/C1, excluding none) in id, title and reason, or reject them at write time in the ticket verb and in the fold.

review.impact: Each successful `werk ticket move`, `archive` or `restore` reads and folds the whole board log three times. `move` calls `readBoard` for `refuseAgentMove` at line 51, `appendBoardEvent` reads and folds the log again, and line 66 reads and folds it a third time only to print the ticket's column. The cost per command grows with the length of the board log, which is append-only and never compacted.
review.fix: Read the log once. `appendBoardEvent` can return the folded board with the new event applied, or accept a board the caller has already folded. The verb then uses that board for `refuseAgentMove` and for the printed column instead of calling `readBoard` again.

Two things in the diff are not asked for by any criterion or user story, though decided cards cover both. (1) src/map/store.ts readMap writes a line to fold-times.jsonl on every read. #pr-log-snapshot-file is one of this ticket's decided cards, so this may stay. (2) The `werk unlink` verb in src/verbs/link.ts is not in any criterion; story 17 (one verb per operation) loosely covers it. Neither is clearly out of scope, so this line passes.

src/verbs/add.ts refuses `--status decided`. The card lets a ghost reach decided before its accept, so this must stay possible through a later status verb. The card does not forbid the refusal in add, so this is not a contradiction.

src/map/store.ts readMap computes `lines` as `text.split("\n").length - 1`. That counts line ends, so when the last log line has no line end (store.test.ts writes such a log) the count is one less than the number of log lines read. Count the lines that are not empty instead.

review.impact: A write checks its events against a map that was folded earlier, by `readMap`, and then appends without a lock. Between that fold and the append it reads the log a second time, but only to check for a trailing newline. If two werk processes write at once (for example two agents), both stamp the same `seq`, and the second write's events are never checked against the first write's events. So the all-or-none, rules-checked append promised in the header comment (#pr-log-refuse) does not hold. The `map` parameter also lets a caller pass a stale or hand-built map.
review.fix: Make `write` own the read-check-append cycle. Under an exclusive lock (a lock file opened with `wx`, or flock), read the log text once, fold it, run `prepare`, compute the lead newline from that same text, and append. Drop the `map` parameter, or keep it only for the caller's own display.

review.impact: The rule for `change.discarded` does not check whether the ghost has ghost children. Only the verb protects them, through `discardSet`. A discard written any other way (a hand-edited log, or a future verb) passes `check`, and `apply` drops the child's refines link, so the ghost child silently becomes a parentless root. This breaks the claim that the rules are 'in one place'.
review.fix: In `ghostRule`, for a discard, refuse when `childrenOf(map, node.id)` is not empty, for example: "#x still has ghost children; discard them first". `discardSet` already writes deepest first, so the verb still passes.

review.impact: No caller tells `Refused` apart from any other error. `runVerb`'s generic catch prints every thrown Error as `werk <verb>: <message>` with exit 1. So a real failure such as EACCES or a TypeError looks just like a rule refusal, and the class exists only to carry a message. The store also writes the CLI word `refused: ` into the message.
review.fix: Either drop the class and throw a plain Error, or make it count: keep the bare rule in `Refused`, add the 'refused:' prefix in the CLI layer, and handle other errors separately (another exit code, or rethrow).

review.impact: `linkRule` checks `why` only for depends_on links. A log line with a non-string `why` on any other link type, such as `{"why": 3}`, passes the rules and is stored. `show` then prints it as-is, while `fieldsRule` rejects the same mistake on node fields.
review.fix: At the top of `linkRule`, add `if (!optionalText(link.why)) return "a link's why is text";`.

review.impact: `text.split("\n").length - 1` counts newline characters, not log lines. When the last line has no line end, a case `write` handles on purpose, the fold-time record undercounts by one, so the `#pr-log-snapshot` timings are off.
review.fix: Count the non-empty lines, for example `text.split("\n").filter((l) => l.trim() !== "").length`, which matches what `fold` folds.

review.impact: discard.ts's run body is the same as accept.ts's (lines 22-32) except for the event type, the actor, the set function and the verb word: read the map, report problems, pick the set when the node is a ghost, write one event per id, print stagedLines. A fix to how a staged change is written or reported has to be made twice, and the two copies can drift apart.
review.fix: Pull the shared steps into one helper, for example `stage(via, id, setOf, type, actor, verb, io)` in a small module beside the verbs, and call it from both verbs. Keep only the --actor gate in accept.ts.

review.impact: Six verb run bodies (show, add, link, unlink, accept, discard) repeat the same three lines: `const log = logPath(); const map = readMap(<verb>, log); io.err(formatProblems(map.problems));`. Each new map verb copies them again, and a change to how problems are reported has to be made in every verb.
review.fix: Add one helper, for example `loadMap(via, io): { log, map }`, that finds the log, folds it and reports the set-aside lines. Call it from each verb.

review.impact: Two refusal messages are written out twice each: "a ghost's words are frozen ..." at lines 57 and 112, and "a real card cannot sit under a ghost ..." at lines 48 and 105. The CLI tests check these strings exactly, so a rewording that misses one copy gives users different text for the same rule.
review.fix: Build each message in one small function, for example `frozen(id)` and `underGhost(id)`, and use it at both places.

review.impact: Each value list is written twice: once as a union type (NodeKind, Status, Who, LinkType) and once as a const array (NODE_KINDS and the others). Adding a kind or a link type means editing two places that nothing ties together. Also, every branch of the Event union repeats `seq; at; actor`.
review.fix: Declare the arrays `as const` and derive the types from them, e.g. `export const NODE_KINDS = ["card", ...] as const; export type NodeKind = (typeof NODE_KINDS)[number];`. Build Event from Draft plus `{ seq: number; at: string }` so the shared fields are written once.

review.impact: Five `as never` casts on the events passed to `step` turn off type checking for those events. A test event that no longer matches the Event shape after a schema change would still compile.
review.fix: Use a typed helper like rules.test.ts's `ev = (draft: Draft) => ({ seq, at: "t", ...draft }) as Event`, or export one from a shared test helper, and drop the `as never` casts.

review.impact: The same `mapOf(...drafts)` fixture builder (number the drafts, JSON.stringify each, fold) is copied in tree.test.ts, show.test.ts, stage.test.ts and rules.test.ts. fold.test.ts has a close variant, and the `card`/`node` draft builders are repeated across files too. A change to the event shape means editing every copy.
review.fix: Move `mapOf` and a `card`/`node` draft builder into one test helper under src/test, for example src/test/map.ts, and import it in each map test.

review.impact: `Refused` is exported, but nothing outside store.ts catches it or checks its type. The CLI's catch in start.ts only reads `.message`, and the class's only other use is a test assertion. It looks like a contract that callers rely on, but none does.
review.fix: Throw a plain Error with the same message, or have a caller actually tell Refused apart from other errors (for example start.ts telling a refused write apart from a crash).

review.impact: The test named "the log lines are one JSON event per line" also checks that an accept of an unknown node is refused, and that an empty event list gives "". These checks are unrelated to the name, so when the test fails the name points the reader to the wrong thing.
review.fix: Move the refusal check into its own test, or into the existing "refuses the whole write" test, so this test asserts only the line format.

review.impact: This test says 'the map is unchanged' but only checks the map's node ids. If copyMap shared the links or ghostEdges arrays with the original, the trial write would push the ghost's refines link into the caller's map and this test would still pass. The fold.test copy test misses it too, because an accept replaces ghostEdges with a new array and that test never checks the original's links. The verbs reuse the same map after write (isLive, stagedLines), so that leak would go unseen.
review.fix: Assert the whole map instead: `expect(map).toEqual(fold(root))`. In fold.test.ts's copy test, also add `expect(map.links).toEqual([{ from: "a", to: "root", type: "refines" }])` after the accept on the copy.

review.impact: node.bodyEdited only checks that the node exists and is not a ghost. A non-string why or body (for example `why: 3`) passes and fold stores it in the map. node.added refuses the same value with "a node's why is text". No test covers this failure path, so the gap is invisible.
review.fix: Check that why and body are optional text for node.bodyEdited, as fieldsRule does. Add a rules.test case expecting `{ id: "a", why: 3 }` to be refused with "a node's why is text".

review.impact: This step discards the real card "a", which the rules refuse, so it changes nothing and no assertion follows it. It looks like it tests that removing a node from the copy leaves the original's nodes alone, but it tests nothing.
review.fix: Propose and discard a ghost on the copy (for example discard "g" before accepting it), then assert `map.nodes.has("g")` is true and `copy.nodes.has("g")` is false. Otherwise remove the line.

review.impact: `logPath("/", {})` reads the real root of the machine running the test, so the result depends on whether `/.werk` exists there. That goes against #werk-test-external and makes the result depend on the host.
review.fix: Test the fallback from a folder inside a fresh temporary directory with no `.werk` in it, and expect `join(thatDir, ".werk", "log.jsonl")`.

review.impact: The `--kind excerpt` refusal only checks the exit code. Any failure that exits with 1, such as a flag parse error, would satisfy it, so it does not prove that the excerpt rule refused the add.
review.fix: Also assert `excerpt.err` equals "werk add: --kind is card, option or source. An excerpt comes only from a quote.\n".

review.impact: `node.bodyEdited` only checks that the node exists and is not a ghost. A log line whose `why` or `body` is a number, object or array still passes, and `apply` writes it onto the node. That breaks the `MapNode` type, which says these fields are strings. `werk show` then prints values like `[object Object]`, and code that later calls string methods on them can throw. Node add/propose checks these same fields through `fieldsRule`, so the two paths do not agree.
review.fix: In `check`, for `node.bodyEdited`, also return "a node's why is text" or "a node's body is text" when `optionalText(event.payload.why)` or `optionalText(event.payload.body)` is false. Add a rules test with a non-string body.

review.impact: `linkRule` checks `why` only for `depends_on` links. On `refines`, `supported_by` and `alternative_to`, a non-string `why` from a hand-edited or foreign log line is kept on the link and printed by `formatNode`. It is the same type hole as above, on links.
review.fix: At the top of `linkRule`, return "a link's why is text" when `link.why` is neither undefined nor a string.

review.impact: `formatNode` and `formatProblems` write titles, bodies, URLs and ids from the log straight to the terminal. The log can come from a cloned repository or be written by an agent. Text that holds ANSI/OSC escape sequences can rewrite what the person sees on screen. For example, it can hide a `proposed` marker or forge the output of a line. Ids are not limited to safe characters either.
review.fix: Strip or escape C0/C1 control characters, except a newline inside body text, before printing log text. Or have `fieldsRule` refuse control characters in `id` and `title`.

review.impact: `readMap` runs `mkdirSync(dirname(path), { recursive: true })` on every read, `werk show` included. When no `.werk` exists in any parent folder, a read-only command makes `.werk/` in the current folder. That folder then catches later `logPath` lookups from every folder below it, so a stray `werk show` in the wrong folder quietly splits the log in two.
review.fix: On a read, write the fold time only when the log's folder already exists: skip the `mkdirSync`, and let the existing try/catch absorb ENOENT. Only `write` should create the folder.

review.impact: Every command folds the whole log. During the fold, each event goes through `check`, and many of the rules call `allLinks`, which copies all live and held links into a new array. `parentOf`, `linksFrom`, `linksTo` and `findLink` each make that copy and scan it. `ancestorsOf` calls `parentOf` once per level, and a refines or depends_on check runs `isAncestor` up to twice. `edge.added` and `edge.removed` also rebuild both link arrays through `drop`. As a result, one step costs O(links × depth), and a full fold costs O(events × links × depth), which is roughly quadratic in the log's length. Each step also creates a lot of short-lived arrays. This cost grows on every add, link, accept, discard and show as the map grows, and the fold time is exactly what `readMap` records.
review.fix: Keep indexes in `FoldedMap` and update them in `apply`: a `parent` map from child id to parent id, plus outgoing and incoming adjacency keyed by id and link type. Answer `parentOf`, `linksFrom`, `linksTo` and `findLink` from these indexes instead of copying `[...links, ...ghostEdges]`. If keeping indexes is too much for now, at least have `linksFrom`, `linksTo` and `findLink` loop over `map.links` and `map.ghostEdges` directly so they stop allocating a copy.

review.impact: `change.accepted` empties `ghostEdges` and places every held link again on each accept. An accept that carries k nodes writes k events, and each one scans and rebuilds the whole held list, so the cost is O(k × held links) per accept command. It also costs this much on every fold of the log.
review.fix: Re-place only the held links that touch the accepted id, using `link.from === id || link.to === id`. Those are the only links that can go live, so the other held links can stay where they are.

review.impact: `write` reads the entire log file again only to see whether it ends with a newline. The caller has just read and folded that same file in `readMap`, so every write reads the full log twice.
review.fix: Check only the last byte. Use `statSync` for the size, then open the file and `readSync` one byte at `size - 1`. Another option is to have `readMap` return or remember whether the text ended with a newline and pass that to `write`.

review.impact: `text.split("\n").length` builds a second array of every log line only to count the lines, after `fold` has already split the same text. This doubles the line-array allocation on every read.
review.fix: Count the newlines without building an array, for example with a loop over `indexOf("\n", from)`. Another option is to have `fold` report how many lines it read.

review.impact: The module-level helper `page()` has the same name as Playwright's `page` fixture. Because of that, every test has to rename the fixture to `p` (`async ({ page: p })`). This differs from the usual Playwright style, and readers can mix up the HTML-string builder with the browser page.
review.fix: Rename the helper, for example to `html()` or `cardDocument()`, and keep the standard `{ page }` fixture name in each test.

review.impact: Only two calls use the `colour()` helper. The rest of the file reads computed colour with an inline `evaluate(el => getComputedStyle(el).color)`, for example at lines 132-136 and 186. With two styles for one operation, the next edit is unlikely to follow either one consistently.
review.fix: Pick one style: either use `colour()` (or a locator-taking variant) for every computed-colour read, or drop the helper and inline it everywhere.

review.impact: The file defines a `colour(p, selector)` helper at line 31, but only the last test uses it. Lines 133-137 (`kw`), 138 (`name`) and 189 (`plain`) write the same `getComputedStyle(el).color` call out by hand instead. That means there are two ways to read a colour, and the next person to add a colour check has to choose between them.
review.fix: Change `colour` to take a Locator, e.g. `colour(locator) => locator.first().evaluate(el => getComputedStyle(el).color)`. Then use it for `kw`, `name`, `plain`, `key` and `str`.

review.impact: The loop variable `link` holds the `<code>` element inside each link, not the link. A reader can easily misread what the monospace check is testing.
review.fix: Rename the variable to `code`. Or select the links and check `link.locator('code')`.

review.impact: The monospace check runs in a loop over `article a[href="/map/al-diff"] code`. If the renderer stopped wrapping the link label in `<code>`, the locator would match nothing and the loop would pass without checking anything. A regression of the monospace label (#werk-reflink-label) would not fail this test.
review.fix: Before the loop, assert the count: `await expect(p.locator('article a[href="/map/al-diff"] code')).toHaveCount(4)`. Or check the computed font-family on each `article a` directly instead of on an optional child.

causeOfLast.why: the cited cards said nothing on archiving an archived ticket, the verb's exit codes or its success output, so an earlier pass made those choices without a card.

grade.gap: pure-files.txt lists src/board/fold.ts, rules.ts, format.ts and events.ts, and each has its own test file. The grader could not run `make test-coverage` here because permission was denied, so this score comes from reading the code. The two guard returns in fold.ts apply() (`if (ticket === undefined) return` for moved, archived and restored) can never run, because refusal() already rejects a ticket that is not on the board. They lower line coverage a little but should not take fold.ts under 90%.

`werk ticket list` and src/board/format.ts go beyond what the acceptance criteria and stories 70 and 74 ask for. They follow the attached decided card #werk-cli-build-ticket-list exactly, so they are left in. Nothing else falls outside the ticket.

Minor: in src/board/rules.ts ARCHIVABLE, archiving from merging is refused. The code cites #werk-board-control, which the builder did not name and which is not among the cards given here; the next pass should confirm that card states it. The archived-row note in format.ts, `from <column>: <reason>`, is inside one helper, so it is not a decision.

review.impact: readBoardLog casts every parsed line to BoardEvent without checking its shape, and the fold only checks that `payload.id` is a string. A line that is valid JSON but the wrong shape throws instead of being set aside. A literal `null` line throws on `event.type` in foldBoard. A `ticket.planned` payload without a `blocked_by` array is accepted, and `openBlockers` then throws on `.filter`. Either way `werk ticket list` and every write crash on one damaged line, which is the case #pr-log-refuse says must not hide the rest of the board.
review.fix: In readBoardLog, send any line that is not an object with a numeric seq and a string type to `unreadable`. In `refusal`, check each event type's payload fields, for example `Array.isArray(blocked_by)`, `typeof title === 'string'` and a valid Column for `to`, and set aside an event that fails with a reason.

review.impact: appendBoardEvent reads the log, folds it, checks the event and then appends, with nothing to stop another writer in between. The server, the command line and the build loop all write this log. Two writers at once can append events with the same seq, or both pass their checks against an old board, for example two moves out of `ready`. The fold then sets one aside, but the writer that was refused was already told it succeeded.
review.fix: Make the read, check and append one step for each writer, for example with an exclusive lock file (`openSync(path + '.lock', 'wx')` with a retry) around the read and the append. Or put the board log under the same single-writer lock as the decision log (#werk-onelock).

review.impact: `refuseAgentMove` runs on its own `readBoard`, and appendBoardEvent then reads and folds the log again. The agent-only rule is checked outside the step that writes, and the log is read twice for one call. The same race as the log.ts finding applies, and the rule sits apart from the other refusals.
review.fix: Pass an extra refusal check into appendBoardEvent, or add an agent-move check that it runs on the board it has already folded, so every rule is checked on the same board that the write is judged against.

review.impact: The column order is written out again here, apart from the `Column` type in events.ts. A column added to the type would be silently missing from `werk ticket list`.
review.fix: Export one `COLUMNS` const array from events.ts, define `Column` as `(typeof COLUMNS)[number]`, and import it in format.ts and rules.ts.

review.impact: `apply` checks `ticket === undefined` for moved, archived and restored, but `apply` only runs after `refusal` has confirmed the ticket exists. These branches can never run, and they hide that `apply` depends on `refusal` running first.
review.fix: Make `apply` private to `tryApply` and narrow `ticket` once with a non-null assertion or invariant, or pass the found `Ticket` in from `refusal`. Then remove the per-case undefined guards.

review.impact: The inline type `{ line: number; reason: string }[]` is written out three times: `Board.unreadable`, the `foldBoard` parameter (line 87) and `BoardLog.unreadable` in `log.ts` (line 17). If the shape changes, all three have to change together.
review.fix: Export a named `Unreadable` type once, for example from `fold.ts` or `events.ts`, and use it in all three places.

review.impact: `COLUMNS` repeats the members of the `Column` union in `events.ts`, and the test helpers repeat them again (the `moved` signature in `rules.test.ts`). A new column added to the type would not show up in `ticket list`, and nothing would flag it.
review.fix: Declare `export const COLUMNS = ["blocked", "ready", "building", "merging", "done"] as const` in `events.ts` and derive `type Column = (typeof COLUMNS)[number]`. Import it in `format.ts` and use `Column` in the test helpers.

review.impact: `b.tickets.get("s/02") as never` is a type escape hatch that switches off checking of the argument.
review.fix: Use a non-null assertion or an explicit `as Ticket`, or check `toBeDefined` first, so the argument is still type-checked.

review.impact: A successful move or archive reads and folds the whole board log three times: in `refuseAgentMove`, inside `appendBoardEvent`, and here to find the column. It also uses `ticket?.column`, which hides the fact that the ticket must exist.
review.fix: Have `appendBoardEvent` return the folded board, or the ticket after the event, alongside the written event, and print its column from that. Alternatively, fold once in the verb and pass the board through.

review.impact: The tests cover only lines that are not valid JSON (`{oops`). A line that is valid JSON but not an object, such as `null`, `42` or `"x"`, is still added to `events`. `foldBoard` then reads `event.type` on `null` and throws a TypeError. That one stray line from a merge would crash `werk ticket list` and every write, because `appendBoardEvent` also runs the fold. This is the case `readBoardLog`'s comment says must not hide the board, and no test catches it.
review.fix: In `readBoardLog`, treat a parsed value that is not a non-null object as unreadable, with a reason such as `not an event`. Add a case to log.test.ts that writes a `null` line and a `42` line between valid events. Assert that each is listed in `unreadable` with its line number, that the events after it still fold, and that `appendBoardEvent` still succeeds.

review.impact: When the ticket is not on the board, `refuseAgentMove` returns undefined and leaves the refusal to `appendBoardEvent`. No CLI test moves an unknown ticket. If someone changed `refuseAgentMove`, or the order of the checks, the exit code or message for `werk ticket move s/09 ready` could regress without any test failing. `werk ticket archive` of an unknown ticket is also untested at the CLI.
review.fix: Add a CLI test: `werk ticket move s/09 ready --reason x` should give `{code: 1, out: "", err: "werk ticket move: ticket s/09 is not on the board\n"}` and leave the board log unchanged. Add the same kind of test for `archive s/09`.

review.impact: readBoardLog only checks that a line is valid JSON, then casts it to BoardEvent. A valid JSON line that is not an object crashes every read of the board. A line such as `null` (from a bad merge or a hand edit) makes `event.type` throw a TypeError at fold.ts:90, so `werk ticket list`, every move, archive and restore, and every appendBoardEvent fail. This breaks the stated rule that one bad line must not hide the rest of the board.
review.fix: After JSON.parse, check that the value is a non-null object with a numeric `seq` and a string `type`. Otherwise push it to `unreadable` with a reason such as 'not a board event' instead of `events`.

review.impact: The fold checks only that `payload.id` is a string (fold.ts:37). A `ticket.planned` event whose `blocked_by` is missing or is not an array still gets applied. The next move of that ticket to building then calls `ticket.blocked_by.filter` and throws, which crashes the command line and the build loop instead of setting the bad event aside.
review.fix: In `refusal`, check the payload's shape for each type: for ticket.planned, `title` is a string and `blocked_by` is an array of strings; for ticket.moved, `to` is a known Column and `reason` is a string or undefined. Return a set-aside reason when the shape is wrong.

review.impact: Ticket titles and move reasons from the board log, and `--reason` from the command line, go to the terminal unchanged. A log line from a merge or an agent can carry ANSI or other control characters, or newlines, that change what the terminal shows or fake extra board rows.
review.fix: Remove control characters (for example `/[\u0000-\u001f\u007f]/g`) from `id`, `title` and `reason` before printing them in `row` and in `formatSetAside`.

review.impact: The next seq is the last event's `seq` plus 1, and the log is never checked. If the last line's `seq` is a string, the `+` joins strings ("x" + 1 gives "x1"), and the appended event gets a seq that is not a number.
review.fix: Use `seq` only when it is a number (`typeof seq === 'number'`), or validate `seq` when reading the log as in the first finding.

review.impact: A `werk ticket move` reads and folds the whole board log three times: once in `readBoard` for `refuseAgentMove`, once inside `appendBoardEvent`, and once more at line 69 to print the column. Archive and restore do it twice. Each read is O(log length), so every command does two to three times the I/O and folding it needs. This grows with the board log, which only grows because it is append-only.
review.fix: Read the board log once. Have `appendBoardEvent` return the folded board after the event, or accept a pre-read `BoardLog`. Then use that board for the `refuseAgentMove` check and for the closing column line, instead of calling `readBoard(path)` again. The column after the write is also known without a read: `column` for a move, and the ticket's existing column for archive or restore.

review.impact: `changes()` only counts `node.decided` as a decide. A `node.added` or `node.proposed` event that carries `status: "decided"` still passes `rules.ts`, and the contract check never sees it. Only the verb layer refuses it today, in the `src/verbs/add.ts:35` guard. So the contract is enforced half in the write path and half in one verb: any other writer that goes through `prepare()` can create a decided card with no who, basis, option or kill criterion. This breaks the rule stated in the `commit.ts` header, which says the write runs the contract check on each card it decides.
review.fix: Make the write path the single place that enforces this. One option: `rules.ts` refuses `status: "decided"` on `node.added`/`node.proposed`, which leaves `node.decided` as the only way to decide a card. The other: `changes()` marks such a node as "decide" so `contractRefusal` checks it. Then the guard in `add.ts` can be removed. If old logs need to fold, apply this only in `prepare()`, not in the fold.

review.impact: `criterionOf` finds the form by looking up flag names that happen to match the `KILL_FORMS` values. This ties the CLI flag names to the data model's form strings. It also silently ignores `--source`, `--threshold` and `--window` when they come without `--metric`, so a mistyped call records a different criterion than the user meant.
review.fix: Map flags to forms explicitly (for example `{ metric: "metric", manual: "manual", "no-metric": "no-metric", revisit: "revisit" }`). Refuse `--source`, `--threshold` and `--window` when the form is not metric.

review.impact: This who check copies the check at line 30 (`who is one of ...`) almost exactly, with an extra `as never` cast. If the who rule or its message changes, one copy can be missed and the two drift apart.
review.fix: Extract a small `whoRule(who: unknown): Rule` helper and call it from both the node.added check and editRule.

review.impact: `RECORDS` writes out the keys of `CardRecords` (types.ts) by hand and is not typed against them. A new record field added to the type will be rejected by editRule as a stray key, and nothing warns you.
review.fix: Type it as `const RECORDS: readonly (keyof CardRecords)[] = [...]` (or derive it with a `satisfies` check) so the compiler ties the list to the type.

review.impact: contractRefusal mixes three branches with no braces, some written as two-line `if`s. It also computes `had`/`lost` for the `decide` and `frozen` cases, which never use them, so it takes a careful read to see that a passing decide or frozen change falls through harmlessly.
review.fix: Use one `if (change === "decide" || change === "frozen") { if (now.length > 0) return ...; continue; }` block before the `had`/`lost` computation, and add braces to the multi-line conditionals.

review.impact: The rewrapped header comment breaks after "and", leaving a short line followed by a dangling continuation. It doesn't match the evenly wrapped comments around it.
review.fix: Rewrap the three comment lines evenly.

review.impact: When one write marks a card "frozen" (a retitle, a body edit or a depends_on change) before it decides that card, `mark` keeps "frozen". The refusal then starts "is decided, and after this change" instead of "cannot be decided". No test puts more than one kind of change to the same card in a single write, so the order in which `mark` ranks the kinds is never checked.
review.fix: Make `mark` rank the kinds as decide > frozen > other, so a decide always wins whatever order the events come in. Add a test in contract.test.ts that calls `refusal(map, retitle, decide)` on an open card that misses facts and expects the header to start "cannot be decided".

review.impact: The tests for `werk status x open` and `werk kill old --revisit --manual x` check only the exit code. If either refusal message broke, or if the code exited 1 for some other reason, the tests would still pass. Nothing tests `werk kill` with no form flag, and nothing checks the `x: edited` output.
review.fix:
Check the stderr text as well: `werk status: the status is decided, not open
` and `werk kill: a criterion names one form: ...
`. Add a test for `werk kill old` with no flag, and check `(await ok(project, ["edit", ...])).out` against `t: edited
`.

review.impact: The tests for frozen links cover only adding a depends_on to a decided card. Nothing tests removing the only depends_on, or the only refines, from a decided card whose basis it was. That path takes the frozen branch of `contractRefusal`, so a wrong mapping in `FROZEN_LINKS` for `edge.removed` would go unnoticed.
review.fix: Add a case where a decided card stands on one depends_on and has no parent and no basis waiver. Remove that edge and expect a "after this change 1 fact is missing\n  basis:" refusal.

review.impact: This change adds `no_basis`, `unchallenged` and `kill` to `MapNode`, but `fieldsRule` checks none of them on `node.added` or `node.proposed`, and `fold.ts:42` spreads the payload straight into the node. A log line that is hand-edited or merged in can therefore carry an empty or non-string waiver, which defeats the written-reason rule for waivers that `editRule` enforces. It can also carry kill criteria that `killRule` would refuse, such as an unknown form or a missing metric word, and the contract check will then accept them. If `kill` is not an array (for example `{}` or a string), the fold does not set the line aside: `[...node.kill]` at `fold.ts:75` throws on the next `kill.added`, and `node.kill.map` at `show.ts:48` throws in `werk show`. Either way the command crashes.
review.fix: In `fieldsRule`, validate the new fields with the same checks as the events that set them. Each waiver must be a non-blank string when present. `kill` must be an array, and `killRule`'s criterion check must accept each entry. Factor that check into a shared `criterionRule`. The other choice is to refuse these keys on `node.added` and `node.proposed`, so that only `node.edited` and `kill.added` can set them.

review.impact: `killRule` checks only the words that the form needs, and `fold.ts:75` stores the criterion object as written. Any extra keys in a `kill.added` payload, such as `__proto__`, large blobs or fields of another form, are kept on the node and carried through copies.
review.fix: Refuse any key that is not `form` or one of that form's `KILL_WORDS`, as `editRule` already does with its stray-key check. Or store a new object built from only the allowed keys.

review.impact: `linksTo` only reads `links` and `ghostEdges`, so a card that an earlier removal already took out does not count as a citer. Example: a and b both cite source s. Remove a, then remove b, and s goes out with b's removal. Restoring a then succeeds, but a's supported_by link to s waits with no message, because s belongs to b's removal. So restoring a removal does not bring back everything that card had when it was removed, and the result depends on which removal is restored first.
review.fix: When deciding whether a source goes, also count citers whose supported_by link is in `map.waiting`: a source that any card cites, in the map or out of it, stays in the map. Or record the shared source in both removals. Add a fold test for remove a, remove b, restore a.

review.impact: This builds the 'is removed with #x; restore #x' message again, a copy of `missing` in rules.ts. If one wording changes, `werk show` and the refusals will name the removal differently.
review.fix: Move the 'removed with' phrase into one exported helper, for example in removal.ts next to `removalHolding`, and use it from both rules.ts and the show verb.

review.impact: `replace` reads as 'swap out', but the function re-places every link. Next to `place`, `drop` and `moveChildren`, the name hides what it does.
review.fix: Rename it to `placeAll` or `replaceLinks`.

review.impact: The verb runs `removalOf` a second time to print its output, separately from the fold that applies the event. The output and the applied removal agree only because `write` happens not to change `map`. If `write` ever starts folding into the map it is given, the output would be computed on the map after the removal and would be wrong.
review.fix: Compute the removal once before calling `write` and use that value for the output. Or read it from a fold of the written events, for example `map.removals.get(id)` on a copy after `step`.

review.impact: This line builds the message for a removed node ("#x is removed with #y; restore #y ...") by hand. `missing()` in src/map/rules.ts:41 builds the same message. If the wording or the rule for naming the removal changes in one place, the two will disagree.
review.fix: Export one formatter from src/map/removal.ts, for example `removedText(map, id)` that returns `#id is removed[ with #holder]` or undefined. Use it in both `missing()` and the show verb, and have each caller append only its own ending ('restore #h first' or 'restore #h to see it').

review.impact: `refusedWithoutActor` repeats the person-only refusal that src/verbs/accept.ts:15-18 still writes inline. There are now two copies of the same text and check.
review.fix: Move `refusedWithoutActor` and `ACTOR_FLAG` into a shared verb helper, for example src/cli or src/verbs/actor.ts, and use them from accept.ts too.

review.impact: `map.removals.get(id) as Removal` is a type cast. It depends on restoreRule having run first and hides that from the compiler. The same cast appears in src/verbs/remove.ts:64. If the order of rule and apply ever changes, this fails at runtime with a TypeError, not a clear error.
review.fix: Narrow the value: `const removal = map.removals.get(id); if (!removal) return;` in fold. In the verb, return the removal from a lookup that throws a clear error.

review.impact: The verb calls `removalOf` again on the map from before the write, so what it prints is computed separately from what the fold applies. For now the two give the same result, but this is the same logic computed twice.
review.fix: Fold the written events onto a copy (or reuse the map that `write`/`prepare` produces) and read `removals.get(id)`, the same way `restore` reads it.

review.impact: `as never` turns off type checking for the event passed to `step`, so the test no longer catches it if the shape of the restore event changes.
review.fix: Build a typed `Event` (`{ seq: 9, at: "t", ...restore("a") } as Event`, or a helper that returns Event) and do not cast to never.

review.impact: The new entry goes at the end of the file, not with the other src/map entries in sorted order. That makes the list harder to scan and merges more likely to conflict.
review.fix: Put src/map/removal.ts between src/map/commit.ts/fold.ts/rules.ts so the src/map block stays in alphabetical order.

review.impact: No fold test removes and then restores a ghost card. A restore runs `replace`, which must put the ghost's refines link and its other links back in `ghostEdges`, not in `links` and not in `waiting`. A bug in that order inside `place` (the node check first, then `isLive`) would pass every current test. The rule tests only check that removing a ghost is allowed (rules.test.ts:239).
review.fix: Add a fold test: propose ghost `g` under `b`, remove `g`, and check that `g` is in `removed` and its links are in `waiting`. Then restore `g` and check that `g` is back in `nodes` with `proposed: true`, its links are back in `ghostEdges`, and `links` holds none of them.

review.impact: At the command-line seam, a refused `remove` is only tested for a missing `--actor`. No test checks that a removal the rules refuse appends nothing to the log and exits with the refusal message: an unknown id, an option, a card that is already removed, or `--reparent` on a root that has children. `restore` has this test (line 181), but `remove` does not.
review.fix: Add a test that runs `werk remove nope --actor you` and `werk remove root --reparent --actor you` on `tree()`. Check exit code 1, the exact `werk remove: refused: ...` message, and that the log keeps the same number of lines.

review.impact: No test has two cards that are both supported_by the same excerpt. `removalOf` takes an excerpt whenever its card goes, even if a card that stays still cites it, and then that card's supported_by link waits. Nothing pins this behaviour, so a later change to it, deliberate or not, would go unnoticed.
review.fix: Add a `removalOf` case where `d` is also supported_by `c:ex0`, and assert the result `taken` that the card asks for, so the behaviour is fixed by a test.

review.impact: The rule that only the person removes or restores is enforced only by the `--actor you` check in src/verbs/remove.ts. `check` accepts `node.removed` and `node.restored` events with `actor: "agent"`. Any other write path, such as a future server endpoint or a batch write, or a log line written by hand, can append an agent-attributed removal, and the fold will apply it. The log would then record removals that the person never made.
review.fix: In `removeRule` and `restoreRule`, refuse when `event.actor !== "you"`, for example by passing `event.actor` into both rules. The write path and the fold then share one gate, and the verb-level `refusedWithoutActor` remains only for the friendlier message.

review.impact: `change.accepted` now calls `replace(map)`, which copies the live links, the held ones and the waiting ones and places each one again. Before this change it placed only `ghostEdges` again. Folding a log now costs O(accepts × all links) instead of O(accepts × held links), so every accept does work that grows with the whole map. Live links never change bucket on an accept, so that work is wasted. Each `edge.added` already scans every link through `drop`, so this only adds to the cost, but accepts are frequent, so the growth adds up on long logs.
review.fix: On an accept, place again only the links that can change bucket. Take `map.ghostEdges`, clear it, and call `place` on each held link, as the old code did. Keep the full `replace` for `node.removed` and `node.restored`, or there re-place only the links that touch the ids those events moved.

The grader could not run `make test-coverage` here because permission was denied, so the gate's output was not seen. The `ticket === undefined` early returns in apply() (src/board/fold.ts) cannot be reached, which costs a few covered lines.

Minor: foldBoard and readBoardLog carry an `unreadable` list of non-JSON lines (src/board/fold.ts Board.unreadable, src/board/log.ts readBoardLog), and only the unbuilt `werk ticket list` would read it. Skipping a bad line is needed so the rest of the board still folds, but carrying the list on Board serves no reader in this ticket.

Several choices cite map cards that are not among the builder's named cards: archive allowed only from blocked, ready or building (src/board/rules.ts ARCHIVABLE, citing #werk-board-control); a blocker not on the board stays open (openBlockers, citing #st-ticket-set-checks); board.jsonl sits beside the decision log's path, WERK_LOG included (src/board/log.ts boardPath, citing #pr-log-where). Each cites a card, so none is unrecorded, but the builder's record should name those cards.

review.impact: Each parsed line is cast straight to `BoardEvent` without checking it. A line that is valid JSON but not an object (`null`, `42`, `"x"`) makes `foldBoard` throw on `event.type`, so `readBoard`, every `werk ticket` call and every later append fail. That is the case the comment above says must not happen ('One bad line ... must not hide the rest of the board'). The decision log already guards against this in `parseLine` (src/map/fold.ts:98).
review.fix: Do what `parseLine` in src/map/fold.ts does: when the parsed value is not an object with a string `type`, add it to `unreadable` with a reason instead of pushing it as an event.

review.impact: `refusal` checks only that `payload.id` is a string. A `ticket.planned` event whose `blocked_by` is not an array is still applied, and the next `refuseMove(..., 'building')` throws in `openBlockers` (`ticket.blocked_by.filter`). A `ticket.moved` with no `to` is also applied, which puts an undefined column on the ticket. A hand-edited or merged line can therefore crash the fold or corrupt the board.
review.fix: Check the payload's shape for each type in `refusal`: `title` is a string, `blocked_by` is an array of strings, and `to` is a Column. Set an event that fails the check aside with a reason, as is already done for a missing id.

review.impact: `appendFileSync` writes the new event straight after the existing text. If the file does not end in a newline (after a hand edit or a merge), the new event joins the last line, so both events become one unreadable line and the earlier event is lost from the board. The decision log's `write` (src/map/store.ts:53-55) adds a leading newline to prevent exactly this.
review.fix: Read the file text once. When it is non-empty and does not end in '\n', add a '\n' before the event, as `write` in src/map/store.ts does.

review.impact: The next seq is the last event's seq + 1. After a union merge of two branches' board logs the last line need not hold the highest seq, so a new event can repeat a seq that is already in the log. `setAside` entries are keyed by seq, so a repeated seq makes them ambiguous. The decision log uses the highest seq it has seen (`lastSeq` in src/map/fold.ts:94).
review.fix: Take the highest numeric seq across the events, for example by tracking `lastSeq` in the fold or computing a max in `readBoardLog`.

review.impact: `Actor` defines `"agent" | "you"` a second time; src/map/types.ts:51 already exports `Actor`. The two can drift apart, for example when an actor is added to one log and not the other.
review.fix: Re-export or import `Actor` from src/map/types.ts (or move it to a shared module) instead of declaring it again.

review.impact: `refusal` already refuses any moved, archived or restored event whose ticket is not on the board. `apply` only runs after that check passes, so the `ticket === undefined` guards in those three cases can never fire. That is dead code: it suggests a state that cannot happen, and it adds branches the 90% coverage gate has to count.
review.fix: Declare `apply`'s precondition that the ticket exists for a non-plan event. Read the ticket with a non-null assertion, or pass in the ticket that `refusal` found, and remove the unreachable guards.

review.impact: The unreadable-line shape `{ line: number; reason: string }` is written out three times: in `Board.unreadable`, in the `foldBoard` parameter and in `log.ts` `BoardLog.unreadable`. If the shape changes, all three copies have to change in step.
review.fix: Export one named type, such as `UnreadableLine`, from fold.ts or events.ts, and use it in all three places.

review.impact: `as never` turns off type checking for the argument to `openBlockers`. If the ticket were missing or had the wrong shape, the type checker would not report it.
review.fix: Use a narrowing helper, such as `const t = b.tickets.get("s/02"); if (!t) throw ...`, or a non-null assertion that keeps the `Ticket` type, instead of `as never`.

review.impact: `refuseAgentMove` repeats the structure of `refusePlan`: the same lookup, the same `OPEN.includes` check and the same message form, with only the suffix changed. Both functions have to change when the rule for an open ticket changes.
review.fix: Pull out one helper, such as `refuseUnlessOpen(board, id, what)`, that returns the shared message with a suffix, and build both functions on it.

review.impact: Header comment line 3 runs well past the wrapping width the rest of the file uses, unlike the other lines. It looks like an insertion that was never reflowed.
review.fix: Reflow the header comment to the same width as the lines around it.

review.impact: readBoardLog only sets aside lines that fail JSON.parse. A line that is valid JSON but not an event object (for example `null`, `42` or `"x"`, which a bad merge could leave behind) goes into `events`. foldBoard then reads `event.type` on null and throws, so readBoard and every `werk ticket` call crash. The test 'a line that is not JSON is set aside' only covers `{oops`, so this path is never tested.
review.fix: Set aside any parsed value that is not an object with a numeric seq and a string type, and give it a reason such as 'not an event'. Add cases with `null` and `42` lines to log.test.ts, and assert that they appear in `unreadable` and that the lines after them still fold.

review.impact: The seq test only covers a log whose last line is a valid event. No test covers a last line that is unreadable, or events whose seq values are not in order. In both cases `events.at(-1)?.seq` can repeat or go backwards, and nothing would catch it.
review.fix: Add a case whose last line is `{oops`, and one where an earlier event has a higher seq than the last. Assert that the next seq is one more than the highest seq in the log, or whatever rule is intended.

review.impact: The CLI tests never run a successful blocked→ready move. They also never move or archive an archived ticket through the verb, so the 'archived; restore it first' path and the 'already archived' path are only tested at the rules level. A wrong mapping in the verb on these paths would go unnoticed.
review.fix: Add a CLI test that moves a blocked ticket to ready and checks the output line and the event. Add one that archives a ticket twice and checks for exit 1 and an unchanged log.

review.impact: readBoardLog only checks that each line parses as JSON. It never checks that the result is an event object. A line that parses to something other than an object, such as `null` (a hand edit or a bad merge resolution can produce one), reaches foldBoard. There `event.type` throws a TypeError, so readBoard, appendBoardEvent and every `werk ticket` call crash. The comment above this function promises that one bad line must not hide the rest of the board, and this breaks that promise.
review.fix: After JSON.parse, check that the value is a non-null object with a numeric `seq` and a string `type`. Send anything else to `unreadable` with a reason such as `not an event`, instead of casting it straight to BoardEvent.

review.impact: refusal() checks only `payload.id`. A `ticket.planned` event whose `blocked_by` is missing or is not an array of strings still folds into the board. Later, `openBlockers` calls `ticket.blocked_by.filter` while checking a move to building, and that throws, so the board can no longer be read or written. For `ticket.moved`, a non-string `reason` is also stored as it is.
review.fix: In refusal(), check each payload's shape before calling the rules. For `ticket.planned`, require a string `title` and an array of strings in `blocked_by`. For `ticket.moved`, require `to` to be one of the columns and `reason` to be a string or absent. Set any event that fails aside with a reason, as the fold already does for an event with no id. The fold stays total over any log content.

review.impact: The next seq is `events.at(-1)?.seq + 1`, read from untrusted file content. If the last event's `seq` is a string, for example `"5"`, this concatenates to `"51"` and writes a seq that is not a number. If it is missing, the result is NaN. Either one corrupts the log's ordering from then on.
review.fix: Compute the next seq from the highest numeric `seq` among the events, for example by filtering with `Number.isInteger`, or validate `seq` when reading as described in the first finding.

review.impact: appendBoardEvent reads the log, checks the rules, then appends, and it holds no lock. Two writers running at once, such as the build loop and an agent's `werk ticket`, can both pass the check against the same board. Both then append events with the same seq, and one may break a move rule. The fold later sets that event aside, but the command already reported success.
review.fix: Hold an exclusive lock while reading, checking and appending, for example with a lockfile created through `openSync(path + '.lock', 'wx')`, or reuse whatever lock the decision log's writer uses.

review.impact: One `werk ticket move` reads and folds the whole board log three times: `readBoard` for `refuseAgentMove` at line 45, `readBoardLog` plus `foldBoard` inside `appendBoardEvent`, and `readBoard` again at line 60 to print the column. Archive and restore do it twice. Each pass is O(n) in the log, and the log only grows, so every command costs a small constant multiple of the work it needs. A CLI call won't notice this, but it is avoidable repeated I/O and parsing.
review.fix: Have `appendBoardEvent` return the board it already folded, with the event applied by `tryApply` (for example `{ ok: true, event, board }`). Print the column from that board and drop the second `readBoard`. Optionally, pass a pre-read board into `appendBoardEvent` so the move path also reuses the board it read for `refuseAgentMove`.

grade.gap: One small extra: `werk show` on a removed node now prints its own refusal, '#x is removed with #y; restore #y to see it' (src/verbs/show.ts, tested in src/verbs/remove.test.ts). No criterion or story asks for this. It does no harm, but the next pass may drop it or tie it to a card.

The diff makes choices that none of the builder's named cards (#werk-remove, #werk-remove-restore-undo, #werk-write-remove-links, #werk-propose-new) gives. Small extras beyond the criteria, all in support of them: one-dash flag forms in src/cli/args.ts and src/cli/help.ts, needed for `-n`. The inbox prints a discarded id with no title (src/map/notes.ts). `-n` must be at least 1, enforced in src/verbs/inbox.ts. None of these is a separate behaviour.

review.impact: The short-flag branch splits one lookup across two `if`s, and the first one tests `short?.value === undefined && short !== undefined`. The reader has to work out that this means 'a switch that was found'. The branch also repeats the value-reading logic that the long-flag path below already has, so the two can drift apart, for example in their error wording.
review.fix: Map `-x` to its spec once, then share one path with `--x`. For example: `const name = /^-[A-Za-z]$/.test(arg) ? arg.slice(1) : arg.startsWith("--") ? arg.slice(2) : undefined`. Then reuse the existing flag lookup, switch handling and value reading, so both forms behave the same.

review.impact: The marker logic assumes that an id with a thread is never proposed while it still has a node. Nothing in `apply` enforces that; it holds only because `rules.ts` refuses a duplicate id. If the rules ever allow re-adding a live id, or if `step` is called with an unchecked event, a stray 'proposed again' marker is added and the inbox mislabels earlier notes.
review.fix: Make the precondition explicit where the marker is pushed: `if (!map.nodes.has(fields.id)) map.threads.get(fields.id)?.push(...)`. Then the fold does not depend on a rule in another module for correctness.

review.impact: `event?.seq` treats an empty result from `write` as possible. If that ever happens, the verb prints `note [undefined] written` and exits 0 instead of reporting a failure.
review.fix: Check the result: if `event` is undefined, write to `io.err` and return a non-zero code. Otherwise destructure without the optional chain.

review.impact: The new one-dash branch copies the long-flag logic for switch versus valued flags: setting a switch to true, taking the next argv entry, the 'needs a value' error, and read(). Its tests are written backwards, as `short?.value === undefined && short !== undefined` and then `short?.value !== undefined`, which hides that these are the two cases of one found flag. Any later change to how flags take values (validation, repeat handling) now has to be made in two places, and the two will drift apart.
review.fix: Resolve the flag spec and its display form once: a short `-x` sets name=arg.slice(1) and eq=-1, and a long one parses `--name[=value]` as now. Then run a single shared block for unknown flag, switch versus value, and missing value. If the branches stay separate, at least write it as `if (short !== undefined) { if (short.value === undefined) {...} else {...} }`.

review.impact: The note.added case rebuilds the thread array with a spread on every note. The node.proposed case a few lines up mutates with `push`, and copyMap already deep-copies each thread array, so the copy here buys no safety. The two cases follow different idioms for the same structure, and folding a long thread costs O(n²).
review.fix: Use the same mutation style as the rest of apply: `const thread = map.threads.get(id) ?? []; thread.push(entry); map.threads.set(id, thread);`.

review.impact: The doc comment says the function returns 'A whole number of at least `least`, or undefined', but it leaves out the `fallback` it returns when the flag is absent. A reader can easily miss that undefined means invalid input, not a missing flag.
review.fix: Reword it, for example: 'The flag as a whole number of at least `least`, `fallback` when it is absent, or undefined when it is not valid.'

review.impact: When a ghost with no notes is discarded, the fold creates an empty thread for its id. If the id is proposed again, the new proposal pushes a lone 'proposed again' marker. `werk show` then prints 'Thread' and a line saying 'the notes above were about the earlier words', with no notes above it. No test covers this path. The fold test 'a first proposal adds no marker' only covers a first proposal, so this behaviour could change or regress without any test noticing.
review.fix: Add a fold/show test for discard, then propose again, on an id with no notes, and assert the intended result. If a lone marker is not intended, create the thread on discard only when one already exists, or add the marker only to a non-empty thread, and assert that `formatNode` prints no Thread section.

review.impact: Only `-n 0` covers the inbox usage-error path. A non-numeric or negative `--since` and a non-numeric `-n` are untested, so a regression in `wholeNumber` for those inputs would pass. One example is accepting `--since -1` or `-n 1.5`.
review.fix: Assert exit code 2 and the usage message for `--since abc`, `--since -1` and `-n x`. A `wholeNumber` unit test would be cheaper than spawning the CLI for each case.

review.impact: The short-flag test does not cover a value flag followed by another flag (`-n -q`). That input silently takes '-q' as the value of n. It also does not pin whether the long form `--n` is still accepted. The new branch in `parseArgs` runs before the long-flag path, so either behaviour could change unnoticed.
review.fix: Add assertions for `parseArgs(inbox, ["-n", "-q"])` and `parseArgs(inbox, ["--n", "5"])` that record the intended results.

review.impact: `indent` handles only `\n`. Note text reaches the terminal unchanged through `werk show` and `werk inbox`, so a note can carry `\r`, ANSI escape sequences or other control characters. An agent's note that holds `\r` can redraw its line in a terminal so that it reads `you: ...` instead of `agent: ...`. In the same way, a stray `\r` or escape in a note the person wrote can corrupt the inbox lines an agent reads and acts on. `rules.ts` checks only that the text is a non-empty string.
review.fix: When printing a note's text, escape or strip C0/C1 control characters other than `\n` (for example, swap `\r`, `\x1b` and similar for a visible stand-in), or refuse them in the `note.added` rule. Add a test with a `\r` and an ESC sequence.

review.impact: The long-form branch still looks up one-letter flag names, so `--n 5` and `--q` are accepted as well as `-n 5`. Help prints only `-n`, so the parser takes a form that is not documented. This is minor input-validation slack.
review.fix: In the `--` branch, refuse a flag whose name is one letter (for example, `return { ok: false, error: `${verb.name} has no flag --${name}` }` when `name.length === 1`), and add that case to `args.test.ts`.

review.impact: Each `note.added` event copies the id's whole thread array (`[...(map.threads.get(id) ?? []), entry]`). Folding a thread of n notes therefore costs O(n²) copies. Every command runs this fold on the full log, so a long-lived card with a busy thread slows down every command.
review.fix: Append in place, the way the `proposed again` marker already does: `const thread = map.threads.get(id); if (thread) thread.push(entry); else map.threads.set(id, [entry]);`. `copyMap` already gives trial writes their own arrays, so the original map is not affected.

review.impact: For every matching note, `entries.slice(index + 1).some(...)` allocates and scans the rest of the thread, so `formatInbox` is O(n²) in thread length. It also runs this for every note after `since`, even though only `count` of them are printed.
review.fix: Find each thread's last `proposed again` seq once, for example by walking the entries backwards and tracking whether a marker has been seen. Then set `earlier = entry.seq < lastMarkerSeq`. That makes the pass linear.
